title: JavaScript fundamentals
blurb: Types, coercion, scope, closures, `this`, hoisting. The phone-screen material — the questions that get asked before anyone looks at your code.

questions.code: console.log("5" + 3, "5" - 3);
questions.why: `+` is overloaded: if either operand is a string it concatenates, so "5" + 3 is the string "53". `-` has no string meaning, so it coerces both sides to numbers and gives 2, not NaN.
questions.asked: The classic opener. It is really testing whether you know `+` is the only arithmetic operator that also does string work.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT falsy?
questions.why: There are eight falsy values (false, 0, -0, 0n, "", null, undefined, NaN), plus the legacy `document.all` in browsers. The string "0" is a non-empty string, so it is truthy, which surprises people reading config values.
questions.asked: Because `if (value)` on a parsed string is a real production bug: "0" and "false" both pass.

questions.why: A bug from the first version of JavaScript that can never be fixed without breaking the web. `typeof` never throws on a value, and "null" is not one of its results. To test for null compare directly: `value === null`.
questions.asked: It is trivia, but it filters people who have never had to write a null check by hand.

questions.code:
const volume = 0;
console.log(volume || 50, volume ?? 50);
questions.why: `||` falls through on any falsy value, and 0 is falsy, so it returns 50. `??` only falls through on null or undefined, so it keeps the deliberate 0. This is exactly why `??` was added.
questions.asked: The single most common real bug this catches: a default kicking in over a legitimate 0 or empty string.

questions.q: What does this equality check log?
questions.why: All JavaScript numbers are IEEE-754 doubles. 0.1 and 0.2 have no exact binary representation, so the sum is 0.30000000000000004. Compare with a tolerance, or store money as integer minor units.
questions.asked: The follow-up is always 'so how would you store a price?', and the answer is cents as an integer, or a decimal type.

questions.why: Each call to makeCounter creates a fresh `count` and a closure over it. `a` and `b` capture different variables, so b's counter starts again at 1 rather than continuing to 3.
questions.asked: This is the standard 'do you understand closures' question. The key insight is one closure per invocation, not one per function.

questions.why: `var` is function-scoped, so all three callbacks close over the same `i`. By the time the timers fire the loop has finished and `i` is 3. Changing `var` to `let` gives a fresh binding per iteration and logs 0 1 2.
questions.asked: It tests closures, the event loop and block scope in four lines. Nearly every interviewer has a version of it.

questions.code:
console.log(x);
let x = 1;
choices: Logs undefined, because the declaration is hoisted
Logs 1, because `let` is hoisted with its value
Throws a ReferenceError from the temporal dead zone
Throws a SyntaxError before any line runs
questions.why: `let` and `const` declarations are hoisted but not initialised; the span before the declaration is the temporal dead zone, and reading there throws. Logging undefined is what `var` would do. It is a runtime error, not a SyntaxError, because the code parses fine.
questions.asked: It separates people who say 'hoisting means var moves to the top' from people who know what actually happens.

questions.q: What is the difference between `==` and `===`?
choices: `==` compares values; `===` also compares memory addresses
`==` converts operands to a common type first; `===` never converts
`===` compares objects by content; `==` compares them by reference
`==` is for primitives only; `===` is required when comparing objects
questions.why: `==` runs the abstract equality algorithm, which coerces, so `"1" == 1` and `null == undefined` are both true. `===` returns false on a type mismatch. Both compare objects by reference, which rules out the content and memory-address answers.
questions.asked: The most-asked JavaScript question in existence. The good answer names a case where the coercion surprises you.

questions.code: console.log([] == false, [] === false);
questions.why: `==` coerces: [] becomes the primitive "", false becomes 0, "" becomes 0, and 0 == 0. `===` sees an object versus a boolean and returns false immediately. This is the strongest argument for always using ===.
questions.asked: It is the punchline that justifies the lint rule, and interviewers want you to walk the coercion steps aloud.

questions.q: In a regular (non-arrow) function, what determines the value of `this`?
choices: The module the function lives in
questions.why: `this` in a normal function is bound at call time: `obj.fn()` binds obj, a bare `fn()` binds undefined in strict mode, and call/apply/bind set it explicitly. 'Where it is defined' is the rule for arrow functions, which capture `this` lexically.
questions.asked: The lead-in to 'why did this break when I passed the method as a callback?'

questions.q: What does this do in an ES module (or any strict-mode code)?
choices: Logs 'hi Ada', since the method remembers `user`
Throws a TypeError, since `this` is undefined
Logs 'hi ', since `this` is the window object
questions.why: Detaching the method loses the receiver, and in strict code a bare call leaves `this` undefined, so reading `.name` throws. Only sloppy scripts substitute globalThis: 'hi undefined' in Node CommonJS, and 'hi ' in a browser classic script because `window.name` defaults to "". Fix with `user.greet.bind(user)` or an arrow wrapper.
questions.asked: It is the same bug as passing `this.handleClick` to an event listener without binding.

questions.q: Which statement about arrow functions is TRUE?
choices: They are shorter syntax with identical semantics
They bind `this` to the object they are written in
They are hoisted like function declarations
questions.why: Arrows take `this` from the enclosing scope and have no `arguments` object or prototype, so they cannot be constructors or methods that need a dynamic receiver. An arrow in an object literal does not get the object as `this`; it gets whatever `this` was outside the literal.
questions.asked: The follow-up is 'so when would you NOT use an arrow function?': object methods and prototype methods.

questions.code: console.log(typeof NaN, NaN === NaN);
questions.why: NaN is a numeric value meaning 'not a valid number', and it is the only value in JavaScript not equal to itself. Test for it with `Number.isNaN()`, never with ===.
questions.asked: The practical follow-up: how do you check whether a parsed input failed?

questions.q: What is the difference between `null` and `undefined`?
choices: `undefined` means never set; `null` is an explicit 'no value'
`null` is what the engine assigns; `undefined` is what you assign
`null` is for objects and `undefined` is for primitives
They are aliases, so `null === undefined` is true
questions.why: The language produces undefined (missing property, no return, unpassed parameter); you produce null deliberately. `null == undefined` is true but `null === undefined` is false, and JSON keeps null but drops undefined.
questions.asked: Because the API contract 'field absent' vs 'field explicitly empty' matters, and JSON treats them differently.

questions.why: Default parameters fire only for `undefined`, not for null or any other falsy value. Passing undefined explicitly is the same as omitting the argument; passing null suppresses the default.
questions.asked: It mirrors the `??` question: 'absent' and 'explicitly empty' are different, and defaults only handle the first.

questions.code: console.log(typeof function () {}, typeof [], typeof class {});
questions.why: typeof has only eight results, and neither 'array' nor 'class' is one. Arrays are objects (use `Array.isArray()`), and classes are functions underneath, so typeof reports function.
questions.asked: Leads directly to 'how do you reliably check whether something is an array?'

choices: It enables newer syntax such as optional chaining and classes
Silent failures throw, and `this` is undefined in bare calls
It lets the engine skip type checks, so code runs faster
It turns on runtime checking of JSDoc type annotations
questions.why: Strict mode makes assigning to an undeclared variable throw, forbids duplicate parameter names, and leaves `this` undefined rather than globalThis in a bare call. New syntax works in sloppy code too. ES modules and class bodies are strict automatically.
questions.asked: Usually as a lead-in to 'why is `this` undefined in my module but not in the console?'

questions.why: `const` prevents rebinding the variable, not mutating the object it points at, so nothing throws. `a` and `b` reference the same object, so the change is visible through both.
questions.asked: It is the root of the React 'why didn't my component re-render' bug and half of all shared-state bugs.

questions.why: `+` has no array meaning, so both sides are converted to primitives, which for an array means `join(",")`. "1,2,3" + "4,5" concatenates to "1,2,34,5". Arrays never concatenate with `+`; that is `concat` or spread.
questions.asked: Nobody writes this on purpose; the point is understanding that every operator falls back to primitive conversion.

questions.q: Which correctly copies an object one level deep?
questions.why: Spread (or `Object.assign({}, original)`) makes a new object with the same top-level values. `new Object(obj)` returns the same object, freeze returns the same object locked, and objects have no `slice`. Nested objects stay shared; for a full copy use `structuredClone()`.
questions.asked: Immediately followed by 'and what happens to nested objects?'

questions.q: What does optional chaining `a?.b.c` do if `a` is null?
choices: Returns undefined for `a?.b`, then throws on `.c`
Short-circuits the whole chain to undefined
Returns null, the value that stopped the chain
Returns an empty object, so `.c` is undefined
questions.why: Once `?.` short-circuits, the rest of the chain is skipped entirely; it does not resume and try `.c`. It always yields undefined, never null. Note it only guards the link it is written on, so `a.b?.c` still throws if `a` is null.
questions.asked: The trap is thinking `?.` protects the whole expression rather than one link.

questions.code:
const obj = { a: 1 };
console.log(obj.toString === Object.prototype.toString);
questions.why: Property lookup walks the prototype chain. `obj` has no own toString, so it finds the one on Object.prototype: the same function object, hence true.
questions.asked: The lead-in to 'why should you use Object.hasOwn or a Map for a lookup table?'

questions.q: You need a lookup keyed by product objects, plus its entry count. Why use a `Map` over a plain object?
choices: Map converts object keys to JSON text, so equal products match
Map keys keep their type and identity, and `size` is built in
Map rejects duplicate values, so each product is stored once
Map entries serialise with JSON.stringify, unlike object keys
questions.why: Plain-object keys are coerced to strings, so every product object becomes "[object Object]" and they all collide; number keys become strings too. Map keys keep their identity, and `map.size` replaces `Object.keys(obj).length`. Map neither serialises its keys to JSON nor deduplicates values.
questions.asked: It tests whether you know object keys are always strings, which is the real reason Map exists.

questions.code: console.log([10, 9, 1, 100].sort());
questions.why: Default sort converts every element to a string and compares those, so "10" sorts before "9". Pass a comparator: `sort((a, b) => a - b)`.
questions.asked: It is the most common array footgun, and sort also mutates in place, which is worth saying.

questions.q: What is a closure, in the shortest accurate form?
choices: A function that has finished running and freed its variables
A function defined inside an object literal as a method
A function whose variables are copied when it is returned
A function plus the variables in scope where it was created
questions.why: The function keeps a live reference to the enclosing scope's bindings, so those variables survive after the outer function has returned. They are shared, not copied: later changes are visible to the closure. That is what makes counters, memoisation and React hooks work.
questions.asked: Universal. What separates answers is whether you can name a real use rather than reciting a definition.

questions.why: `var x` is hoisted to the top of the function, so the inner `x` shadows the outer one for the whole body, and at the log it is declared but not yet assigned, hence undefined. A ReferenceError would need `let` (the temporal dead zone).
questions.asked: It is the cleanest demonstration of why `var` was replaced.

choices: Spread iterates grapheme clusters; `.length` counts bytes
`.length` counts UTF-8 bytes, and the emoji takes two of them
Spread iterates code points; `.length` counts UTF-16 code units
Spread drops the emoji's variation selector; `.length` keeps it
questions.why: String iteration yields code points, so a surrogate pair (most emoji) counts once, while `.length` counts UTF-16 units, so '👋' alone is 2. Neither counts user-perceived characters: combined emoji and combining marks still split, which needs `Intl.Segmenter`.
questions.asked: It comes up whenever a character-count feature has to handle emoji.

questions.q: What is the difference between a function declaration and a function expression?
choices: An expression is hoisted whole and callable before its line
A declaration is hoisted whole and callable before its line
A declaration is block-scoped; an expression is always global
Only an expression can be passed to another function as a value
questions.why: `function f() {}` is hoisted whole. `const f = function () {}` only binds when that line runs, so calling it earlier hits the temporal dead zone; with `var f = function () {}` the name exists as undefined and the call is a TypeError. Both kinds are values you can pass around.
questions.asked: A standard warm-up that leads into hoisting.

questions.code:
const { a = 1, b = 2 } = { a: undefined, b: null };
console.log(a, b);
questions.why: Destructuring defaults follow the same rule as parameter defaults: they apply only to undefined. `b` is explicitly null, so the default is skipped.
questions.asked: It catches people who assume defaults handle 'empty' generally.

choices: Its own properties are locked; nested objects stay mutable
The object and every nested object become read-only
It returns a frozen copy and leaves the original mutable
Writes to it throw a TypeError in every mode, sloppy included
questions.why: freeze is shallow and in place: `Object.freeze({ inner: { n: 1 } })` still lets you set `.inner.n = 2`. Writes to a frozen property are silently ignored in sloppy mode and throw only in strict code. A deep freeze means recursing yourself.
questions.asked: Because 'we froze the config so it's safe' is a claim that is often wrong.

questions.code: console.log(typeof typeof 1);
questions.why: typeof always produces a string, so typeof of that string is "string". Pure trivia, but a fast way to check whether someone is reasoning or pattern-matching.
questions.asked: A speed check: it shows whether you evaluate inside-out or guess from the last token.

questions.q: Which of these mutates the array it is called on?
questions.why: splice, push, pop, shift, unshift, sort, reverse and fill all mutate. slice, concat, map, filter and the newer toSorted/toReversed/with return new arrays.
questions.asked: Directly relevant to React: mutating state in place is why a component fails to re-render.

questions.q: What is the practical difference between `for...in` and `for...of`?
choices: `for...in` gives array values; `for...of` gives the indexes as numbers
`for...in` gives enumerable keys, inherited too; `for...of` gives values
`for...in` gives own keys only; `for...of` adds the inherited keys
`for...of` works on plain objects; `for...in` works only on arrays
questions.why: `for...in` over an array gives index *strings* and walks the prototype chain, so it is the wrong tool for arrays. `for...of` needs an iterable, and plain objects are not iterable. Use `for...of` for values and `Object.entries()` for an object's own pairs.
questions.asked: The bug it prevents: someone adds a helper to Array.prototype and every for...in loop in the codebase changes behaviour.

questions.why: `let` creates a fresh binding on every iteration, so each arrow closes over its own `i`. Swapping in `var` gives [3, 3, 3].
questions.asked: The counterpart to the setTimeout question: it checks you know why `let` fixes it, not just that it does.

questions.q: Why is `Number()` usually safer than `parseInt()` for query-string input?
choices: parseInt still reads a leading 0 as octal, so '08' becomes 0
parseInt returns a string, so later arithmetic concatenates
parseInt stops at the first invalid character, so '12abc' is 12
parseInt throws on non-numeric input and crashes the handler
questions.why: parseInt parses as far as it can and ignores the rest, so '12abc' silently becomes 12, while `Number('12abc')` is NaN, the failure you want. Leading-zero octal guessing was removed in ES5. Number is not a full validator either: `Number('')` is 0, so still reject empty input.
questions.asked: Relevant every time you read a query-string parameter.

questions.q: What does the spread operator do with a string?
questions.code: console.log([...'abc']);
questions.why: Strings are iterable, so spread produces an array of characters (code points), not char codes. It is the shortest way to split a string into characters while keeping surrogate pairs together.
questions.asked: A quick check that you know strings are iterable, which is the basis for most character-level loops.

questions.why: Private fields (#) are genuinely private: not enumerable, not reachable from outside, and invisible to Object.keys or JSON.stringify. `value` is a prototype accessor, so it is not an own key either.
questions.asked: Follow-up to 'how do you make a field private in JavaScript?': the old answer was closures or a leading underscore convention.

questions.q: What happens when this runs as an ES module?
choices: It logs dev, because a plain assignment overrides it
It logs prod, because the write is silently ignored
It throws a TypeError at the assignment line
It logs undefined, because the property is hidden
questions.why: `defineProperty` defaults `writable`, `enumerable` and `configurable` to false, so `env` is read-only. Modules are strict, and in strict code writing a read-only property throws. Silently ignoring it is the sloppy-script behaviour, which is why this bug hides in old code.
questions.asked: Descriptors explain frozen objects, getters and library internals; the strict vs sloppy split shows real depth.

questions.code: console.log(Object.is(-0, 0), Object.is(NaN, NaN), -0 === 0);
questions.why: `Object.is` is SameValue: it tells -0 and 0 apart and treats NaN as equal to itself, the two places it differs from `===`. React uses it to decide whether state changed.
questions.asked: It usually comes up as 'how does React compare state?', and the precise answer is Object.is.

choices: It logs Save, then `render()` returns Save as well
It logs Save, then `render()` throws a TypeError
It logs undefined, then `render()` throws a TypeError
questions.why: The arrow field is created per instance in the constructor, so it captures that instance's `this` and survives being detached. `render` lives on the prototype and gets `this` from the call; class bodies are strict, so a bare call leaves it undefined and `this.label` throws. The price of the arrow field is one function per instance.
questions.asked: It explains why class components bound handlers, and whether you know the memory cost of the arrow-field fix.

questions.why: JSON.stringify serialises own enumerable properties, and a class getter lives on the prototype, so `full` is not included. Add a `toJSON()` method or map to a plain object if the API must return it.
questions.asked: A computed field vanishing from an API response is a real bug, and this checks you know where getters live.

questions.why: Strings are immutable: `trim()` returns a new string and leaves `input` alone, and the result is thrown away here, so the length is still 7. You need `const email = input.trim()`. Nothing throws, even though `input` is const, because nothing is reassigned.
questions.asked: A junior screen staple: it checks you know string methods return values rather than changing the string.

questions.q: You split a CSV line with an empty field. What does this log?
questions.code:
const parts = 'a,b,,c'.split(',');
console.log(parts.length, parts[2]);
questions.why: `split` keeps empty fields between adjacent separators, so the result is ['a', 'b', '', 'c']: four parts, and index 2 is the empty string, not undefined. That is usually what you want for CSV, where an empty column still has a position.
questions.asked: Parsing delimited input is a common take-home task, and off-by-one column bugs start here.

questions.q: Two ids arrive as strings from the URL. What does this log?
questions.why: When both operands are strings, `<` compares them character by character, and '1' comes before '9', so '10' < '9' is true. Only when one side is a number does it convert both to numbers. Convert ids with `Number()` before comparing.
questions.asked: Sorting or comparing numeric strings from query params is a quiet source of wrong results.

questions.q: What is the last value this loop logs?
choices: b, since the loop stops early
questions.why: Indexes run from 0 to length - 1, so `i <= items.length` does one extra pass with i = 3. Reading past the end of an array gives undefined rather than throwing, so the bug is silent. The condition should be `i < items.length`, or use `for...of`.
questions.asked: The classic off-by-one; interviewers also want to hear that out-of-range reads do not throw in JavaScript.

questions.why: `continue` skips the rest of the current iteration and moves on to the next one, so even numbers are skipped and 1 and 3 are logged. `break` would stop the loop entirely and log only 1.
questions.asked: Basic control flow, used to check you can trace a loop precisely before harder questions.

questions.code: console.log(parseFloat('3.99 EUR'), Number('3.99 EUR'));
questions.why: `parseFloat` reads as much of a number as it can from the start and ignores the rest, so it returns 3.99. `Number` requires the whole string (after trimming whitespace) to be numeric, so the currency suffix makes it NaN.
questions.asked: Picking the right parser for user-entered prices and quantities is a daily form-handling decision.

questions.q: What happens when a request body contains `{name: 'Ada'}` and you call `JSON.parse` on it?
choices: It returns `{ name: 'Ada' }`, since JSON accepts JS literals
It returns undefined, since the input is not valid JSON
It throws a SyntaxError, since keys and strings need double quotes
It returns the input unchanged as a string
questions.why: JSON is stricter than JavaScript object syntax: keys must be double-quoted and strings use double quotes, so this input throws a SyntaxError. JSON.parse never returns undefined for bad input; wrap it in try/catch and answer with a 400.
questions.asked: Handling malformed input without crashing the server is basic API hygiene.

questions.why: With a string pattern, `replace` changes only the first match. Use `replaceAll('-', '/')` (ES2021) or a regex with the `g` flag to change every occurrence.
questions.asked: It is the most common string-method surprise, and it shows up in date and slug formatting code.

questions.q: The URL is `?page=2`. What does this log?
questions.code:
const page = new URLSearchParams('?page=2').get('page');
console.log(page + 1);
questions.why: URLSearchParams values are always strings, so `+` concatenates '2' and 1 into '21'. Convert first with `Number(page)`, and handle a missing param, which `get` returns as null.
questions.asked: The 'next page' button that jumps to page 21 is a real bug; this checks you know query params are strings.

questions.why: `for...of` over a string visits each character, and `(counts[ch] || 0) + 1` starts a missing key at 0, so 'l' reaches 2. A key that was never set reads as undefined, not 0 or null.
questions.asked: Counting things in a loop is the most common junior live-coding task; the follow-up is doing it with a Map.

questions.q: What happens when you run `for (const x of { a: 1 }) {}`?
choices: It loops once, with x set to the value 1
It loops once, with x set to the key 'a'
It throws a TypeError: the object is not iterable
It runs zero times, since objects have no length
questions.why: `for...of` requires an iterable (arrays, strings, Maps, Sets), and plain objects do not implement `Symbol.iterator`, so it throws. Loop over `Object.keys`, `Object.values` or `Object.entries` instead; `for...in` is the loop that walks object keys.
questions.asked: It checks you know which loop fits which data shape before you write one in a live exercise.

questions.why: indexOf returns the position, and a match at the very start is 0, which is falsy, so the else branch runs. A miss is -1, which is truthy. Use `includes` (or compare against -1) when you only need yes or no.
questions.asked: A real bug in search and validation code that only fails when the match is at position 0.

questions.code: console.log(Number(''), Number(' 42 '), Number('4 2'));
questions.why: Number trims surrounding whitespace, so ' 42 ' is 42, and an empty or all-whitespace string converts to 0 rather than NaN. Inner spaces make the string invalid. So an empty form field silently becomes 0 unless you check for it first.
questions.asked: It is the follow-up to 'use Number, not parseInt': the strong answer knows Number's own blind spot.

questions.q: You remove every 2 while looping forward. What does this log?
questions.why: splice shifts the next element into index i, and then `i++` steps past it, so the second 2 is never checked. Loop backwards, or better, build a new array with `ids.filter((n) => n !== 2)`.
questions.asked: Mutating a collection while iterating it is a classic bug in every language, and interviewers want the filter answer.

questions.code:
const price = (1.005).toFixed(2);
console.log(price, typeof price);
questions.why: toFixed returns a string, and 1.005 is stored as 1.00499999999999989…, so it rounds down to '1.00'. For money, keep integer minor units and format at the edge, or use `Intl.NumberFormat`.
questions.asked: Invoice totals that are a cent off are a real support ticket; this checks you know why.

questions.q: A feature flag may or may not be declared by an injected script. What does this log when `betaFlag` was never declared anywhere?
questions.code: console.log(typeof betaFlag);
questions.why: `typeof` is the one operator that tolerates an undeclared identifier and returns the string "undefined" instead of throwing. Reading `betaFlag` any other way would throw a ReferenceError, which is why old feature-detection code used `typeof x !== 'undefined'`.
questions.asked: It checks whether you know the difference between an undeclared variable and one that holds `undefined`.

questions.q: A CSV import passes these strings through two parsers. What does this log?
questions.code: console.log(Number('1e3'), Number('0x1F'), parseInt('0x1F'), parseInt('1e3'));
questions.why: `Number()` accepts the full numeric-literal grammar, so exponent and hex strings both convert. `parseInt` reads leading digits: it recognises a `0x` prefix (radix 16) but stops at the `e` in '1e3', giving 1. That silent truncation is why '1e3' imported through `parseInt` becomes 1, not 1000.
questions.asked: Interviewers use it to see whether you can explain why two 'string to number' functions disagree, rather than treating them as interchangeable.

questions.code: console.log(isNaN('abc'), Number.isNaN('abc'));
questions.why: The global `isNaN` coerces its argument to a number first, so 'abc' becomes NaN and it returns true. `Number.isNaN` does no coercion and only returns true for the actual NaN value, so a string gives false.
questions.asked: A quick check that you reach for `Number.isNaN` and know why the global version gives false positives on strings.

questions.code: console.log(Number.isInteger(5.0), Number.isSafeInteger(2 ** 53));
questions.why: JavaScript has one number type, so 5.0 is the same value as 5 and counts as an integer. 2 ** 53 is an integer but it is one past `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`, where adjacent integers stop being distinguishable, so it is not 'safe'.
questions.asked: It leads into the real question: what happens to 64-bit database ids when they pass through a JavaScript number.

questions.q: Two order ids come back from a Java service as JSON numbers. What does this comparison log?
choices: It throws a RangeError while parsing
questions.why: Both literals round to the same double, 9007199254740992, because integers above 2^53 cannot all be represented. `JSON.parse` does not throw; it silently loses precision, so two different orders compare equal. The fix is to send large ids as strings.
questions.asked: Teams with Snowflake-style or 64-bit ids hit this for real; a strong answer says 'serialise ids as strings' without being prompted.

questions.q: You are splitting 7 items across pages of 2. What does this log?
questions.code: console.log(7 / 2, Math.floor(7 / 2), 7 % 2);
questions.why: `/` is always floating-point division in JavaScript, so 7 / 2 is 3.5; there is no integer division operator. `Math.floor` gives the whole pages and `%` the remainder, 1. Page counts need `Math.ceil(7 / 2)`, which is 4.
questions.asked: Pagination maths is everywhere in CRUD work, and people coming from C# or Java expect `7 / 2` to be 3.

questions.q: A charge of 2.5 pence and a refund of -2.5 pence each go through the rounding helper. What does this log?
questions.code: console.log(Math.round(2.5), Math.round(-2.5));
questions.why: `Math.round` rounds halves towards positive infinity, not away from zero, so 2.5 becomes 3 but -2.5 becomes -2. Refunds and negative adjustments therefore round differently from charges unless you round the absolute value and reapply the sign.
questions.asked: It shows up whenever credits or refunds are rounded; knowing the asymmetry is what separates 'I tested positives' from 'I tested the domain'.

questions.q: A carousel steps backwards with `index = (index - 1) % slides.length`. With `index` 0 and 3 slides, what is the new index?
choices: -1, because `%` keeps the sign of the left side
questions.why: JavaScript's `%` is a remainder, not a mathematical modulo: the result takes the sign of the dividend, so -1 % 3 is -1 and `slides[-1]` is undefined. The wrap-safe form is `((i % n) + n) % n`.
questions.asked: Off-by-one wrap bugs in carousels, pagers and circular buffers all trace back to this; interviewers like the `((i % n) + n) % n` fix.

questions.why: Division by zero never throws in JavaScript. A non-zero number divided by zero gives a signed Infinity, and 0 / 0 is NaN. An 'average per order' with zero orders therefore produces NaN on the dashboard rather than an error you would notice.
questions.asked: It checks you guard empty denominators yourself, because the language will not stop you.

questions.q: A basket totals prices such as 19.99 and 0.10. Which representation avoids floating-point drift in the total?
choices: Store each price as a string and add them with `+`
Store each price as a number rounded with `toFixed(2)`
Store integer minor units, such as 1999 pence
Store each price as a float and round only when saving
questions.why: Integers up to 2^53 are exact in a double, so adding pence never drifts; you convert to pounds only for display. `toFixed` returns a string and rounds at the wrong moment, and strings with `+` concatenate rather than add.
questions.asked: Money handling is a standard CRUD interview topic, and 'integer minor units' is the answer they are listening for.

questions.q: A Vitest assertion `expect(0.1 + 0.2).toBe(0.3)` fails. Which change makes the test correct rather than just green?
questions.why: `toBeCloseTo` compares within a tolerance (two decimal places by default), which is the honest assertion for a float result. `toEqual` uses the same equality for numbers as `toBe`, so it still fails, and converting to a string gives '0.30000000000000004'.
questions.asked: It tests whether you understand float error well enough to write assertions about it, not just to recite 0.1 + 0.2.

questions.code:
const subtotal = (0.1 * 3).toFixed(2);
console.log(subtotal + 1);
questions.why: `toFixed` returns a string, "0.30", so `+ 1` concatenates and gives "0.301". Round for display at the very end, and keep the value a number (ideally integer minor units) while you are still calculating.
questions.asked: It is the most common way a rounded price quietly turns into string concatenation in a basket total.

questions.code:
const user = { name: 'Ada' };
console.log(`Saved ${user}`);
questions.why: Template literals convert the value with its string conversion, which for a plain object is `Object.prototype.toString`, giving "[object Object]". `console.log(user)` prints the structure only because the console inspects objects itself.
questions.asked: It explains the '[object Object]' that appears in toasts and log lines, and the fix is `user.name` or `JSON.stringify(user)`.

questions.why: Both use ToPrimitive with a different hint. Binary `+` uses the 'default' hint, which for ordinary objects tries `valueOf` first, so it gets 5 and adds 1. A template literal uses the 'string' hint, which tries `toString` first, giving '£5'.
questions.asked: Deep coercion questions separate people who memorised a table from people who know that ToPrimitive has hints; it also explains how `Date` behaves.

questions.q: Two bookings start on the same day. What does this log?
questions.why: `==` between two objects compares references, and these are two different Date objects, so it is false. Relational operators convert both to numbers via `valueOf`, so `<=` compares timestamps and is true. Compare instants with `getTime()`.
questions.asked: Date equality bugs are common in booking and scheduling code; the answer shows you know objects compare by reference.

questions.code:
const d = new Date(2026, 11, 25);
console.log(d.getMonth(), d.getDate(), d.getDay());
questions.why: Months are zero-based, so 11 is December and `getMonth` returns 11. `getDate` is the day of the month, while `getDay` is the weekday (0 = Sunday); 25 December 2026 is a Friday, so 5.
questions.asked: Zero-based months and the `getDate`/`getDay` naming trap cause real off-by-one bugs in date pickers.

questions.q: A subscription renews 'one month after 31 January'. What does this log?
questions.why: Date setters do not clamp: 31 February 2026 overflows by three days into 3 March, so month 2, day 3. Billing code has to clamp to the last day of the target month itself (or use a library or Temporal, which clamps by default).
questions.asked: It is a real billing bug, and a strong answer mentions clamping or Temporal's `add({ months: 1 })`.

questions.q: A form posts a date typed as '31/12/2026'. What happens here in Node 24?
choices: Logs 2026, then an ISO string for 31 December
Throws a SyntaxError on the first line
Logs NaN, then throws a RangeError
questions.why: The constructor never throws on unparseable input; it creates an Invalid Date whose getters return NaN. `toISOString` is the method that throws (RangeError: Invalid time value), often far from where the bad input entered. Validate with `Number.isNaN(d.getTime())`.
questions.asked: It checks that you validate dates at the boundary instead of discovering an Invalid Date when serialising the response.

questions.code: console.log(null + 1, undefined + 1);
questions.why: Numeric conversion turns null into 0 but undefined into NaN, so the results are 1 and NaN. That asymmetry is why a missing field (undefined) poisons a sum while an explicit null does not.
questions.asked: A quick probe of whether you know null and undefined convert differently, which matters when summing optional fields.

questions.code: console.log(null == 0, null >= 0);
questions.why: Loose equality has a special rule: null is only `==` to null and undefined, so `null == 0` is false. Relational operators instead convert to numbers, turning null into 0, so `null >= 0` is true. The two operators do not share an algorithm.
questions.asked: It is a favourite 'explain the spec' question; the strong answer names the separate `==` and relational algorithms.

questions.code: console.log(true + true, '3' * '4');
questions.why: With no string operand, `+` converts booleans to numbers, so true + true is 2. `*` has no string meaning, so both strings convert to numbers and the result is 12, not concatenation.
questions.asked: A warm-up that confirms you know only `+` concatenates and every other arithmetic operator converts to numbers.

questions.q: A quantity input's `value` is used in a running total. What does this log?
questions.why: `0 + '2'` concatenates to '02' because one side is a string, and then '02' + 3 concatenates again to '023'. Form values are always strings; convert with `Number()` or read `input.valueAsNumber` before doing arithmetic.
questions.asked: It is the most common form-handling bug in beginner CRUD code, so interviewers want to hear 'input values are strings'.

questions.why: The loose-equality algorithm treats null and undefined as equal to each other and to nothing else, with no numeric or string conversion. That makes `x == null` a deliberate, lint-approved shorthand for 'null or undefined', unlike a truthiness check that also rejects 0 and ''.
questions.asked: It is the one place many style guides allow `==`; knowing why shows you understand the algorithm rather than avoiding it by rule.

questions.q: In a CommonJS script without "use strict", what does this log?
questions.why: Primitives cannot hold properties. The assignment briefly wraps 'GBP' in a String object, sets the property on that throwaway wrapper, and discards it, so the read finds nothing. In strict mode (and in ES modules) the same assignment throws a TypeError.
questions.asked: It tests the primitive/wrapper model behind `'abc'.length` working at all, and the strict-mode difference is the bonus point.

questions.code:
const s = new String('draft');
console.log(typeof s, s === 'draft', s == 'draft');
questions.why: `new String` creates a wrapper object, so `typeof` is 'object' and strict equality with a primitive is false. Loose equality unwraps it via ToPrimitive and compares 'draft' with 'draft'. Calling `String(x)` without `new` returns a primitive, which is what you almost always want.
questions.asked: It checks you know why `new String`, `new Number` and `new Boolean` are lint errors.

questions.q: Ids arrive as strings and someone converts them in one line. What does this log?
questions.code: console.log(['10', '10', '10'].map(parseInt));
questions.why: `map` passes (value, index, array), so the calls are parseInt('10', 0), parseInt('10', 1) and parseInt('10', 2). Radix 0 means 'default' (10), radix 1 is invalid (NaN), and '10' in binary is 2. Use `.map(Number)` or an explicit arrow.
questions.asked: Beyond the trivia, it tests that you know callbacks receive more arguments than you might think.

questions.q: A dashboard shows the highest order value. With no orders yet, what does this log?
questions.code:
const totals = [];
console.log(Math.max(...totals));
questions.why: `Math.max()` with no arguments returns -Infinity, the identity value for 'maximum', so spreading an empty array does not throw or give 0. Guard the empty case explicitly before rendering.
questions.asked: Empty-collection handling is a mid-level habit; the answer shows you think about 'no data yet' states.

questions.q: The URL has no `size` parameter. What does this log?
questions.why: `get` returns null for a missing key and `Number(null)` is 0, a real number, so `??` never falls back. Apply the default before converting (`Number(params.get('size') ?? 20)`) or validate the parsed value.
questions.asked: Defaulting query parameters is daily API work, and the order of 'default then convert' is exactly what reviewers catch.

questions.q: Two reports sum the same line items in a different order. What does this log?
choices: It depends on the V8 version
questions.why: Floating-point addition is not associative: each step rounds, so 0.1 + 0.2 + 0.3 is 0.6000000000000001 while 0.3 + 0.2 + 0.1 is 0.6. IEEE 754 makes this deterministic across machines; it is not hardware noise. Summing integer minor units removes the problem.
questions.asked: It explains why two reports can disagree by a penny, and the answer 'rounding happens at every step' shows real understanding.

questions.q: What does this log for a guest (`isMember` is false)?
questions.why: `+` binds tighter than `?:`, so the condition is the whole string 'Price: false', which is non-empty and truthy. The expression therefore always yields 'member', without the prefix. Parenthesise the ternary or use a template literal.
questions.asked: Operator-precedence bugs like this survive code review because they read naturally; spotting it quickly is the point.

questions.q: In a sloppy-mode script, what does this log?
questions.why: Strings are immutable primitives, so assigning to an index is silently ignored in sloppy mode (and throws in strict mode). String methods always return a new string: capitalise with `status[0].toUpperCase() + status.slice(1)`.
questions.asked: It checks you know strings are immutable, which is why every string method returns a new value you must keep.

questions.code:
const file = 'report.csv';
console.log(file.slice(-3), file.substring(-3));
questions.why: `slice` treats a negative index as counting from the end, so -3 gives 'csv'. `substring` clamps negative arguments to 0, so `substring(-3)` returns the whole string. Prefer `slice` whenever you need from-the-end offsets.
questions.asked: It shows whether you know the two look-alike methods differ in exactly the case you need for file extensions.

questions.q: Invoice numbers must be three digits wide. What does this log?
questions.code: console.log(String(7).padStart(3, '0'));
questions.why: `padStart(targetLength, padString)` adds padding at the start until the string reaches the target length, so '7' becomes '007'. If the string is already long enough, it is returned unchanged, not truncated.
questions.asked: A practical formatting question for ids, times and receipts; mentioning that it never truncates is a nice extra.

questions.code:
const date = '2026-01-05';
console.log(date.replaceAll(/-/, '/'));
questions.why: `replaceAll` requires a regex argument to carry the `g` flag and throws a TypeError otherwise, precisely so a non-global regex cannot look like it replaced everything. Use `/-/g` or pass the string '-'.
questions.asked: It checks that you know `replace` with a string only changes the first match and how `replaceAll` guards the regex case.

questions.q: A table filter must match 'Admin' when the user types 'admin'. Which check is correct?
questions.why: `includes` and `search` are case-sensitive, so both sides must be normalised to the same case first. `localeCompare` returning 0 checks whole-string equality in sort order, not a substring match, and is case-sensitive by default too.
questions.asked: Client-side search boxes are a staple take-home task; case-insensitive matching is the first thing a reviewer tries.

questions.q: A cookie-style string is parsed into a key and value. What does this log?
questions.code:
const [key, value] = 'token=abc123=='.split('=');
console.log(value);
questions.why: `split('=')` splits on every '=', producing ['token', 'abc123', '', ''], so the base64 padding is lost. Split once instead: find the first index with `indexOf('=')` and `slice` either side, or use `URLSearchParams` for query-style data.
questions.asked: Base64 values and tokens routinely contain '=', so this is a real parsing bug interviewers like to see spotted.

questions.q: Why can a SQL library safely support `` sql`SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ${id}` `` as a tagged template?
choices: The engine escapes quotes inside every template literal automatically
The tag function gets the literal parts and `id` separately, so it can send `id` as a bound parameter
Tagged templates are evaluated lazily, after the query plan is compiled
The `${}` value is converted with `JSON.stringify` before insertion
questions.why: A tag function receives an array of the fixed string parts plus the interpolated values as separate arguments, so the library builds `... WHERE id = $1` and sends the value out-of-band. A plain template literal with no tag just concatenates, which is exactly SQL injection.
questions.asked: It connects a language feature to security; strong candidates explain that the danger is concatenation, not the backticks.

questions.q: A list of product names is sorted with the default comparison. What does this log?
questions.code: console.log('apple' < 'Banana', 'Zebra' < 'apple');
questions.why: String comparison uses UTF-16 code unit values, and every uppercase ASCII letter (65–90) sorts before every lowercase one (97–122). So 'Banana' comes before 'apple' and 'Zebra' does too. Use `localeCompare` or `Intl.Collator` for human ordering.
questions.asked: It explains why a sorted list shows all capitalised names first, which users report as a bug.

questions.q: A user registered as 'café' on a Mac and logs in typing 'café' on another device. What does this log?
questions.why: 'é' can be one precomposed code point (U+00E9) or 'e' plus a combining acute accent (U+0301); they render the same but are different strings. `normalize()` converts both to the NFC form, after which they compare equal. Normalise usernames and search keys on the way in.
questions.asked: Unicode normalisation bites login, search and de-duplication; mentioning NFC at the input boundary is the strong answer.

questions.q: A character counter must show 1 for the family emoji '👨‍👩‍👧', which has `.length` 8. Which expression gives 1?
questions.why: The emoji is five code points (three people joined by two zero-width joiners), so spreading gives 5 even after normalisation, and `TextEncoder` counts UTF-8 bytes (18). `Intl.Segmenter` splits text into grapheme clusters, the user-perceived characters, giving 1.
questions.asked: Counters and truncation in chat or bio fields hit this; knowing code units, code points and graphemes are three different things is the point.

questions.q: A preview truncates messages to four characters. What does this log?
questions.code:
const msg = 'Hi 👋 there';
console.log(JSON.stringify(msg.slice(0, 4)));
questions.why: `slice` counts UTF-16 code units and the emoji takes two, so cutting at 4 keeps only its first half, a lone surrogate that renders as a broken glyph. Truncate by graphemes with `Intl.Segmenter` (or at least by code points with `[...msg]`).
questions.asked: Broken emoji in notification previews is a real bug report; this checks you can explain it in terms of UTF-16.

questions.q: A role check reuses one regex. What does this log?
questions.code:
const isAdmin = /admin/g;
console.log(isAdmin.test('admin'), isAdmin.test('admin'));
questions.why: With the `g` (or `y`) flag, `test` is stateful: it starts at `lastIndex` and advances it after a match. The second call starts at index 5, past the end, fails, and resets `lastIndex` to 0. Drop `g` for yes/no checks.
questions.asked: Intermittent validation failures from a shared global regex are a classic 'works every other time' bug.

questions.q: Why does this US ZIP code check accept 'abc123456'?
questions.code:
const isZip = (s) => /\d{5}/.test(s);
console.log(isZip('abc123456'));
choices: `\d` also matches letters when the `u` flag is missing
`test` coerces the string to a number first
The pattern has no `^` and `$`, so any five digits inside match
questions.why: Without anchors a regex matches anywhere in the string, so '12345' inside the input is enough. Validation patterns need `^\d{5}$` to say 'the whole string is exactly five digits'. `{5}` does mean exactly five repetitions, but only of that part of the pattern.
questions.asked: Unanchored validators are one of the most common regex bugs in form and API validation.

questions.why: Named capture groups `(?<name>...)` appear on `match.groups`, and captures are always strings, so the month is '09' rather than the number 9. Named groups keep parsing code readable compared with `m[2]`.
questions.asked: It checks you know named groups exist and that every capture is a string you still have to convert.

questions.q: You need every `#tag` in a post along with its capture group for the tag name. Which call gives you both for all matches?
questions.why: With the `g` flag, `match` returns only the full match strings and drops capture groups. `matchAll` returns an iterator of full match objects, groups and index included. A single `exec` returns only the first match.
questions.asked: Extracting mentions, tags or tokens is common, and knowing why `match` with `g` loses groups saves a lot of confusion.

questions.code:
const line = 'price: 10, tax: 2';
console.log(line.replace(/\d+/g, (n) => n * 2));
questions.why: When the replacement is a function it is called once per match (the `g` flag makes it all matches) with the matched text, and its return value is converted to a string. '10' * 2 converts to a number, so the result is 20, and likewise 4.
questions.asked: Replacer functions come up in template engines and data masking; it checks you know they exist.

questions.q: A greeting template does `template.replace('{name}', user.name)`. A user named `$&Co` sees 'Hello {name}Co'. Why, and what is the fix?
choices: `$&` is a replacement pattern for the matched text; pass `() => user.name` instead
`replace` treats its first argument as a regex; escape the braces with `RegExp.escape`
`$` starts a template literal inside strings; wrap the name in backticks
`replace` HTML-decodes the input; encode the name with `encodeURIComponent`
questions.why: Replacement strings interpret `$&`, `$1`, `$<name>`, `` $` `` and `$'` even when the search is a plain string. A replacer function's return value is inserted literally, so it is the safe way to insert user-controlled text.
questions.asked: It is a subtle data-corruption bug in hand-rolled templating, and a strong answer knows replacement patterns apply to string searches too.

questions.q: A search box builds `new RegExp(query, 'i')`. What happens when a user searches for 'c++' in Node 24, and what is the fix?
choices: It matches 'c' followed by any characters; wrap the query in quotes
It matches literally because `RegExp` escapes strings; nothing to fix
It returns no matches; add the `u` flag
It throws a SyntaxError; build it with `RegExp.escape(query)`
questions.why: User input becomes regex syntax, and '++' is an invalid quantifier ('Nothing to repeat'), so the constructor throws. `RegExp.escape` (Node 24, recent browsers) escapes every metacharacter; for a plain substring search, `includes` avoids regex entirely.
questions.asked: Unescaped user input in a regex is both a crash and a ReDoS vector; knowing `RegExp.escape` now exists is current knowledge.

questions.q: What does the `(?=.*\d)` part of `/^(?=.*\d).{8,}$/` do in a password rule?
choices: It requires at least one digit without consuming any characters
It requires the password to start with a digit
It forbids digits anywhere after the eighth character
It captures the first digit into group 1
questions.why: `(?=...)` is a lookahead: it asserts that `.*\d` could match from this position, then rewinds, so `.{8,}` still sees the whole string. Lookaheads let you stack independent rules in one pattern; they do not capture.
questions.asked: Password-policy regexes are a common interview artefact; explaining 'asserts without consuming' shows you actually read them.

questions.q: Which validation pattern can hang a Node server on a crafted 40-character input?
questions.why: Nested quantifiers such as `(\w+\s?)+` can split the same text in exponentially many ways, so a near-match that fails at the end makes the backtracking engine explore all of them (ReDoS). Because the event loop is single-threaded, one request blocks everyone.
questions.asked: ReDoS is a real Node CVE class; interviewers want 'nested quantifiers plus single-threaded event loop' in the answer.

questions.q: Why does a name field validated with `/^[a-z]+$/i` reject 'Zoë', and what fixes it?
choices: The `i` flag ignores accents; remove it
`$` needs the `m` flag to see the end
questions.why: `[a-z]` is a code-point range covering ASCII letters only, and case-insensitivity does not add accented letters to it. Unicode property escapes such as `\p{L}` (any letter) require the `u` or `v` flag.
questions.asked: Rejecting real names is an accessibility and inclusivity bug; knowing `\p{L}` is the modern fix.

questions.q: A log parser looks for a block that spans lines. What does this log?
questions.code:
const log = 'BEGIN\nstep 1\nEND';
console.log(/BEGIN.*END/.test(log), /BEGIN.*END/s.test(log));
questions.why: By default `.` matches any character except line terminators, so the pattern cannot cross the newlines. The `s` (dotAll) flag makes `.` match newlines too. The `m` flag is different: it changes what `^` and `$` anchor to.
questions.asked: It checks you can tell the `s` and `m` flags apart, which people routinely mix up.

questions.q: A settings field lists tags separated by commas and inconsistent spaces. What does this log?
questions.code: console.log('red, green,blue ,  pink'.split(/\s*,\s*/));
questions.why: `split` accepts a regex, and `\s*,\s*` consumes the comma along with any whitespace around it, so each piece comes out trimmed. Splitting on ',' alone would leave the spaces attached.
questions.asked: Parsing loosely formatted user input is everyday work; a regex separator is the tidy answer.

questions.q: An API handler serialises a partially filled record. What does this log?
questions.code: console.log(JSON.stringify({ name: 'Ada', phone: undefined, fax: null }));
questions.why: JSON has no undefined, so object properties whose value is undefined are omitted entirely, while null is a real JSON value and is kept. A PATCH body built this way cannot distinguish 'leave phone alone' from 'clear phone' unless you send null.
questions.asked: It matters for PATCH semantics, where omitted and null mean different things.

questions.code: console.log(JSON.stringify([undefined, () => 1, NaN, Infinity]));
questions.why: Inside arrays, values JSON cannot represent become null so that indexes are preserved; in objects, undefined and functions are dropped instead. NaN and Infinity have no JSON literal and are always written as null, so a failed calculation silently becomes null in the response.
questions.asked: It explains mysterious nulls in API responses, which usually come from NaN in a calculation.

questions.why: `Date` has a `toJSON` method that returns an ISO string, but `JSON.parse` has no idea the string was a date, so it stays a string. Every date in an API response is a string until you convert it (or use a reviver).
questions.asked: It checks you know dates never survive JSON as dates, which is why client code calls `new Date(...)` on API fields.

questions.q: A row from a Postgres driver has a `bigint` id returned as a BigInt. What happens when the handler runs `res.json(row)`?
questions.code:
const row = { id: 42n, name: 'Ada' };
console.log(JSON.stringify(row));
choices: It throws a TypeError about BigInt
questions.why: `JSON.stringify` throws 'Do not know how to serialize a BigInt' rather than guessing, because converting to a number could silently lose precision. Convert explicitly, usually to a string, or configure the driver to return strings.
questions.asked: Anyone who has returned Postgres `bigint` columns from Node has hit this; the fix discussion is what interviewers want.

questions.why: If a value has a `toJSON` method, `JSON.stringify` serialises whatever it returns instead of the object. Here that is the string '19.99', so it is quoted. This is the same hook `Date` uses to become an ISO string.
questions.asked: It checks you know how to control a value object's wire format without mapping every response by hand.

questions.code:
const user = { id: 1, name: 'Ada', passwordHash: 'x9f...' };
console.log(JSON.stringify(user, ['id', 'name']));
choices: It throws, because the replacer must be a function
questions.why: When the second argument is an array, it is an allow-list of property names to include (applied at every nesting level). It works, but an explicit response DTO is safer than remembering to pass the list every time.
questions.asked: Leaking fields like password hashes is a real incident; interviewers like hearing about allow-lists and DTOs.

questions.q: A misbehaving client sends a body with a repeated key. What does this log?
questions.code:
const body = JSON.parse('{"role":"user","role":"admin"}');
console.log(body.role);
questions.why: `JSON.parse` accepts duplicate keys and the last one wins. Other parsers may keep the first or reject the document, so a proxy and your API can disagree about the same payload; validate with a schema and never trust a role from the body.
questions.asked: Parser differentials are a real security topic, and the question checks you know JSON.parse's rule.

questions.q: Which call turns the ISO `createdAt` strings in a parsed API response back into `Date` objects?
questions.why: The second argument to `JSON.parse` is a reviver called for every key and value, bottom-up, and whatever it returns replaces the value. An array allow-list is a `stringify` feature, there is no options object, and `structuredClone` copies the strings as strings.
questions.asked: It checks you know the reviver hook exists; strong candidates add that schema libraries such as Zod usually own this conversion.

questions.q: A settings endpoint merges the request body into defaults. What does this log?
questions.why: `JSON.parse` creates an ordinary own property named '__proto__', so `body.isAdmin` is undefined. `Object.assign` copies with assignment, which triggers the `__proto__` setter on the target and makes the attacker's object its prototype, so `settings.isAdmin` is inherited as true.
questions.asked: Prototype pollution through merge helpers is a recurring Node CVE; explaining why parse is safe but assign is not is the deep answer.

choices: It loops until the stack overflows
It throws a TypeError about a circular structure
questions.why: `JSON.stringify` tracks the objects it is visiting and throws 'Converting circular structure to JSON' when it meets one again. JSON is a tree format, so graphs such as ORM entities with back-references need a DTO or a replacer.
questions.asked: It usually comes up when an ORM entity with a back-reference is returned straight from an endpoint.

questions.q: A hand-edited config file ends with `{"port": 3000,}`. What does `JSON.parse` do with it?
questions.why: JSON does not allow trailing commas (or comments, or single quotes), even though JavaScript object literals do. Formats such as JSONC or JSON5 relax this, which is why `tsconfig.json` can have comments but your API payloads cannot.
questions.asked: It checks you know JSON is stricter than JavaScript literal syntax.

questions.code: console.log(typeof JSON.stringify(undefined), typeof JSON.stringify(null));
questions.why: `JSON.stringify(undefined)` returns undefined itself, not a string, because undefined is not representable; `null` serialises to the string 'null'. Code that writes the result to a file or response then writes nothing or the text 'undefined'.
questions.asked: It explains empty or 'undefined' response bodies from handlers that stringify a missing value.

questions.q: What does the third argument in `JSON.stringify(config, null, 2)` do?
choices: Keeps only the first two properties
Indents the output with two spaces per level
Rounds numbers to two decimal places
questions.why: The third argument is `space`: a number of spaces (up to 10) or a string used to indent each nesting level, for human-readable output. The second argument, the replacer, is null here meaning 'no filtering'.
questions.asked: A basic check that you can produce readable JSON for logs, fixtures and config files.

questions.q: In Node 24, how can code recover the exact digits of a 20-digit number while parsing JSON, before it is rounded to a double?
choices: Pass `{ bigint: true }` as the second argument to `JSON.parse`
Call `BigInt()` on the parsed number afterwards
Read `context.source`, the third argument passed to a reviver
questions.why: Node 24 supports the JSON.parse source text access proposal: a reviver receives a third `context` argument whose `source` is the raw text of primitive values, so you can build a BigInt or keep a string. After parsing, the digits are already lost, so `BigInt(value)` just converts the rounded double.
questions.asked: It is current platform knowledge; the strong answer still says 'better to send big ids as strings' in the first place.

questions.why: `const` makes the binding permanent: `cfg` must always point at the same object. It says nothing about that object's contents, which stay mutable. Use `Object.freeze` (shallowly) or readonly types if the contents must not change.
questions.asked: It checks you can separate 'the variable cannot be reassigned' from 'the value is immutable'.

choices: It logs 3000, and the assignment is ignored
It throws a TypeError at the assignment
It throws a SyntaxError before running
questions.why: Assigning to a `const` binding throws 'TypeError: Assignment to constant variable' at runtime, when the line executes; it is not a parse-time error and is not silently ignored, even in sloppy mode.
questions.asked: A warm-up on `const` semantics; mentioning that it is a runtime TypeError is the precise answer.

questions.why: `let` and `const` are block-scoped, so `draft` does not exist outside the braces, and `typeof` on an undeclared name gives 'undefined'. `var` is function-scoped and ignores the block, so `saved` is visible.
questions.asked: It confirms you know why `var` leaks out of blocks and why modern code avoids it.

questions.q: What happens when this file runs?
choices: Throws a SyntaxError and logs nothing
questions.why: Redeclaring a `let` in the same scope is an early error, detected when the file is parsed, so no line runs at all. `var` allows redeclaration, which is one of the reasons it hid bugs.
questions.asked: It distinguishes parse-time (early) errors from runtime errors, a distinction that matters when reading stack traces.

questions.q: In a CommonJS file without "use strict", what does this log?
questions.why: In sloppy mode, assigning to an undeclared identifier creates a property on the global object, so a typo or missing `let` leaks state across the whole process. Strict mode (and every ES module) throws a ReferenceError instead.
questions.asked: Accidental globals leaking between requests on a Node server is a real bug; strict mode is the fix they want to hear.

choices: It throws a SyntaxError on declaration
questions.why: The inner `const status` shadows the outer one for the whole function body, including its own initialiser. Reading it there is a read inside the temporal dead zone, so it throws 'Cannot access status before initialization'. Rename one of the variables.
questions.asked: It tests that you know scope is decided at parse time for the whole block, not line by line.

questions.why: Function declarations are hoisted along with their body, so `save` is callable from the top of the scope. With a function expression only the `var` declaration is hoisted, initialised to undefined, and the function is assigned when that line runs.
questions.asked: It checks you can predict hoisting for both forms rather than recite 'declarations are hoisted'.

choices: It creates the user, because classes are hoisted like functions
It throws a ReferenceError, because the class is in its TDZ
It throws a TypeError: User is not a constructor
It creates an object without the `name` property
questions.why: Class declarations are hoisted like `let`: the name is reserved for the whole scope but not initialised until the declaration runs. Using it earlier throws a ReferenceError, unlike a function declaration.
questions.asked: A good follow-up to function hoisting; it catches people who assume classes are sugar for function declarations in every respect.

questions.code:
console.log(typeof token);
let token = 'abc';
choices: It logs 'undefined', like any undeclared name
It logs 'object', because the value is null
questions.why: `typeof` only tolerates names that are not declared at all. `token` is declared by `let` in this scope, so the read happens in its temporal dead zone and throws, even inside `typeof`.
questions.asked: It is the sharpest TDZ question: the candidate has to reconcile it with `typeof` on an undeclared variable returning 'undefined'.

questions.q: Why does this reducer fail to load at all?
choices: `break` cannot follow a declaration on the same line
The whole `switch` body is one block, so `msg` is declared twice
`switch` compares with `==`, so the cases overlap
questions.why: All cases share the single block of the `switch`, so two `let msg` declarations collide and cause a SyntaxError. Wrap each case body in its own braces: `case 'add': { let msg = ...; break; }`.
questions.asked: Reducers and command handlers use `switch` constantly; the braces-per-case habit is what interviewers look for.

questions.q: Loaded as an ES module in Node 24, what does this log?
questions.why: Each ES module has its own top-level scope, so even `var` and function declarations stay local to the module. In a classic (non-module) browser script, the same code would create `window.appName` and `window.helper`.
questions.asked: It shows you understand module scope as the thing that ended accidental globals, not just an import syntax.

questions.why: The returned arrow closes over `done`, a variable that lives as long as the closure does. The first call flips it to true, so later calls skip `fn`. Each call to `once` creates a separate `done`.
questions.asked: Writing `once` is a standard closure exercise, and explaining where `done` lives is the real answer.

questions.why: Closures capture variables, not snapshots of their values. When `applyDiscount` runs it reads the current value of `discount`, which is 0.5 by then.
questions.asked: The 'variables, not values' distinction is the core of every closure bug, so interviewers test it directly.

questions.q: A long-running Node API wraps `getUserById` in a naive `memoize` that stores every result in a `Map` forever. What is the main risk?
choices: The Map will be garbage-collected between requests
Unbounded memory growth, and stale users after updates
Every call will hit the database twice
questions.why: The closure keeps the Map alive for the life of the process, so every distinct id adds an entry that is never evicted, and cached users never see later edits. Production caches need a size limit (LRU), a TTL, or invalidation on write.
questions.asked: It checks you see memoisation as a cache with the usual size and invalidation problems, not a free speed-up.

questions.q: Does the returned closure keep `bigRows` in memory for as long as `handler` is registered?
choices: Yes; closures copy every variable in their scope
No; only `count` is referenced, so V8 retains just that
Yes, until the page reloads, even if `handler` is removed
Yes; arrow functions retain their caller's arguments object
questions.why: V8 keeps only the variables a closure actually references in its context, so `rows` can be collected once `track` returns. The retention problem appears when some closure created in the same scope does reference `rows`: sibling closures share one context, so it lives as long as any of them.
questions.asked: It separates a myth ('closures capture everything') from the real mechanism, shared context objects, which is what causes actual leaks.

questions.why: `snapshot` is a local copied from `count` when `makeLogger` ran, so it stays 0. `count` itself is read live when `log` runs, so it is 5. This is exactly the 'stale closure' shape behind stale state in React handlers and timers.
questions.asked: Stale closures are the root of many React bugs; this checks you can reason about which value a closure will see.

questions.q: `createAccount()` declares `let balance = 0` and returns `{ deposit, getBalance }`. Can calling code set `balance` directly?
choices: No; `balance` is only reachable through the returned closures
No, but only because the returned object is frozen
questions.why: `balance` is a local variable of `createAccount`, not a property of the returned object, so assigning `account.balance` just creates an unrelated property. Only the functions created inside the factory can read or change it: closure-based privacy.
questions.asked: It checks you know closures were JavaScript's privacy mechanism long before `#private` fields.

questions.why: Only a `for (let ...)` header creates a fresh binding per iteration. Here `i` is declared once outside the loop, so every closure shares the same variable, which is 3 by the time they run.
questions.asked: It checks you know why `let` fixes the classic loop bug, rather than believing `let` is magic everywhere.

questions.why: The methods reach `n` through their closure, not through `this`, so pulling `get` off the object does not break it. That is a practical advantage of closure-based modules over methods that depend on `this`.
questions.asked: It contrasts closure-based state with `this`-based state, which matters when functions are passed around as callbacks.

questions.why: `withTax(0.2)` returns a new function that remembers `rate` in its closure. Calling it with 100 gives 120, and a separate call creates a separate closure with rate 0.05. This is partial application, a common way to configure functions once.
questions.asked: It checks you can read a function that returns a function, which appears in middleware, validators and selectors.

questions.q: In a hand-written `debounce(fn, ms)`, why is `let timer` declared in `debounce` rather than inside the returned function?
choices: So it is shared across calls and each call can cancel the previous timeout
So it is garbage-collected after every call
Because timers cannot be created inside arrow functions
So each call gets a fresh timer that never clears the others
questions.why: Debounce works by clearing the previous pending timeout and starting a new one. That needs one `timer` variable that outlives each call, which is exactly what the closure over `debounce`'s scope provides; a local inside the returned function would be new every time.
questions.asked: Writing debounce is an interview staple; explaining where the timer lives shows you understand why it works.

questions.why: JavaScript evaluates default parameter expressions on every call where the argument is undefined, so each call gets a new array. Python evaluates defaults once, which is where the shared-list expectation comes from.
questions.asked: Developers coming from Python often expect the shared-default bug; knowing JavaScript differs shows precise knowledge.

questions.why: Parameters and their defaults are evaluated in their own scope, created before the function body runs, so `region` in the default refers to the outer 'eu'. The body's `let region` is a separate binding that the default cannot see.
questions.asked: It is a deep scope question; the strong answer mentions that parameter lists get their own scope.

questions.q: A logging helper must accept any number of arguments as a real array. Which signature does that in modern code?
questions.why: Rest parameters collect the remaining arguments into a genuine array with `map`, `filter` and friends. The old `arguments` object is array-like rather than an array, and arrow functions do not have their own `arguments` at all.
questions.asked: It checks you know rest parameters replaced `arguments`, and why arrows cannot use the old approach.

questions.code:
const toRow = (id) => { id: id };
console.log(toRow(7));
questions.why: After `=>`, a `{` starts a function body, so `id:` is parsed as a statement label and `id` as an expression statement; nothing is returned. To return an object literal from a concise arrow, wrap it in parentheses: `(id) => ({ id })`.
questions.asked: Mapping rows into objects with arrows is everyday code, and this parse surprise produces arrays of undefined.

questions.q: Which of these functions is pure?
questions.why: A pure function's result depends only on its arguments and it changes nothing outside itself. `stamp` mutates its input and reads the clock, `next` changes outer state, and `load` depends on a database; only `total` is pure.
questions.asked: Pure functions are easy to test and cache; interviewers want you to name both parts of the definition.

questions.q: A file has no semicolons. What happens when it runs?
choices: Throws a SyntaxError at parse time
Logs nothing; the function is never called
Throws a TypeError: 10 is not a function
questions.why: Automatic semicolon insertion only adds a semicolon when the next line cannot continue the statement. A line starting with `(` can continue it, so the code parses as `10(function...)` and throws when calling the number. Leading-parenthesis lines need a semicolon in no-semicolon styles.
questions.asked: Teams using no-semicolon styles hit this; knowing the rule, not just 'always use semicolons', is the stronger answer.

questions.why: `return` is a restricted production: a line break straight after it inserts a semicolon, so the function returns undefined and the object literal below is unreachable code (parsed as a block with a label). Keep the returned expression on the same line as `return`.
questions.asked: It is the classic ASI trap, and explains why formatters put the opening brace on the `return` line.

questions.q: A recursive `flattenComments` works in tests but crashes in production on a thread nested 50,000 levels deep. What is the error, and the usual fix?
choices: RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded; rewrite it with an explicit stack
A TypeError on the deepest comment; add optional chaining
An infinite loop; track visited comments in a Set
questions.why: Each recursive call uses a stack frame, and V8's stack holds on the order of ten thousand frames, so very deep input overflows it. Converting to a loop with your own array as a stack moves the depth onto the heap. JavaScript engines do not perform tail-call optimisation in practice.
questions.asked: Tree-shaped data (comments, categories, org charts) is common in CRUD apps; this checks you know recursion has a real limit.

questions.q: What does the first line of output look like?
questions.code: [10, 20].forEach(console.log);
questions.why: `forEach` calls its callback with (element, index, array), and `console.log` prints every argument it receives. Passing a function reference hands it all three arguments, which is harmless here but breaks functions with optional parameters such as `parseInt`.
questions.asked: It checks you know array callbacks receive three arguments, the root of several 'point-free' bugs.

questions.q: In Node 24 (CommonJS), what does this log?
questions.why: The callback is a regular function called by the timer machinery, not by `timer`, so its `this` is not `timer` (in Node it is the Timeout object; in browsers it is `window`). `++undefined` is NaN. An arrow function would inherit `this` from `start` and log 1.
questions.asked: Lost `this` in callbacks is the most common `this` bug; the arrow-function fix is what interviewers expect.

questions.q: What is the difference between `fn.call(ctx, a, b)` and `fn.apply(ctx, [a, b])`?
choices: `call` runs now; `apply` returns a bound function
Only the argument format: a list versus an array
`apply` ignores `ctx` inside arrow functions; `call` does not
`call` copies the arguments; `apply` passes them by reference
questions.why: Both invoke the function immediately with `this` set to `ctx`; `call` takes the arguments individually and `apply` takes them as one array. `bind` is the one that returns a new function. For arrow functions, neither can change `this`.
questions.asked: A standard warm-up; a good answer also places `bind` alongside and mentions spread made `apply` less necessary.

questions.why: A bound function's `this` is fixed permanently. Binding it again creates a wrapper whose `this` is 'B', but that wrapper calls the first bound function, which ignores the `this` it receives and uses 'A'.
questions.asked: It tests whether you understand bound functions as wrappers, which also explains why `new` is the only thing that overrides `bind`.

questions.q: In an ES module, what happens here?
questions.why: Arrow functions take `this` from the surrounding scope, and an object literal does not create one, so `this` is the module's top-level `this`, which is undefined in ES modules; reading `.items` throws. Use method shorthand, `count() { return this.items; }`.
questions.asked: It checks you know arrows are the wrong tool for object methods, the mirror image of the callback bug.

questions.q: An Express route is registered as `router.get('/users', controller.list)`. What happens on the first request?
choices: It works, because class methods are auto-bound
It returns an empty JSON array
Express binds `this` to the router, so `this.service` is undefined
It throws a TypeError, because `this` is undefined inside `list`
questions.why: Passing `controller.list` passes a bare function, so Express calls it without a receiver. Class bodies are strict mode, so `this` is undefined and reading `.service` throws. Register `controller.list.bind(controller)`, an arrow wrapper, or define `list` as an arrow class field.
questions.asked: This is the backend version of the lost-`this` bug, and it shows up in real controller code.

questions.q: In a sloppy-mode CommonJS script, someone forgets `new`. What does this log?
questions.why: Called without `new`, a sloppy-mode function gets the global object as `this`, so it writes a global `name` and returns undefined. In strict mode `this` is undefined and the assignment throws, and class constructors refuse to run without `new` at all.
questions.asked: It explains why classes and strict mode exist: they turn a silent global write into an error.

questions.q: In a sloppy-mode CommonJS script, what does this log?
questions.why: `print` is called as a method, so its own `this` is `report`, but the inner regular function gets a fresh `this` from how `map` calls it: undefined, which sloppy mode turns into the global object, which has no `title`. An arrow callback would inherit `print`'s `this`.
questions.asked: It checks you know every regular function has its own `this`, even when nested inside a method.

questions.q: Which name refers to the global object in browsers, Web Workers and Node alike?
questions.why: `globalThis` was standardised (ES2020) precisely because each environment had its own name: `window` in pages, `self` in workers and `global` in Node. Code shared between server and client should use `globalThis`.
