questions.asked: Useful for isomorphic code and tests; it is a quick check of how current your knowledge is.

questions.why: `apply` spreads the array into individual arguments, so this is `Math.max(3, 7, 2)`. `Math.max` does not use `this`, so passing null is fine. Today `Math.max(...values)` says the same thing more clearly.
questions.asked: You will see `apply` in older code; the question checks you can read it and know the spread equivalent.

questions.code:
const log = console.log.bind(console, '[api]');
log('ready');
questions.why: `bind` fixes `this` and also pre-fills leading arguments (partial application), so every call to `log` passes '[api]' first. That makes it a quick way to build a prefixed logger.
questions.asked: It checks you know `bind` does partial application, not only `this` fixing.

questions.why: `Object.create(base)` makes `base` the prototype, so `greet` is found by walking up the chain, and `this` is still `user` because of how it was called. `Object.keys` lists only own enumerable properties, so the inherited method is not included.
questions.asked: The basic prototype-chain lookup question; a good answer separates 'where the method lives' from 'what `this` is'.

questions.why: Reading walks up the prototype chain, but assigning creates or updates an own property on the object itself. `prefs.theme = 'dark'` shadows the inherited value and leaves `defaults` untouched.
questions.asked: It checks you know reads and writes treat the prototype chain differently.

questions.why: `a.items.push` reads `items` (found on the prototype) and mutates that single shared array; it never assigns to `a.items`. Every instance sees the change. Per-instance state belongs in the constructor or class fields, not on the prototype.
questions.asked: Shared mutable state on a prototype is a real bug in older codebases; it tests reads-vs-writes on the chain.

questions.why: `for...in` walks enumerable properties up the prototype chain (own first), while `Object.keys` returns only own enumerable keys. That difference is why `for...in` loops over objects built with `Object.create` or polluted prototypes pick up unexpected keys.
questions.asked: It checks you know why linters push `Object.keys`/`Object.entries` over `for...in`.

questions.q: A lookup table of user-supplied words is created with `Object.create(null)`. What does this log?
questions.code:
const dict = Object.create(null);
console.log('toString' in dict, typeof dict.hasOwnProperty);
questions.why: An object with a null prototype inherits nothing, so keys such as 'toString', 'constructor' or '__proto__' behave like ordinary data. The trade-off is that methods like `hasOwnProperty` are missing, so use `Object.hasOwn(dict, key)`.
questions.asked: Null-prototype dictionaries are a standard defence when keys come from users, and interviewers like the `Object.hasOwn` follow-up.

questions.why: Methods are defined once on `Row.prototype` and shared, whereas a class field is evaluated per instance, so every row gets its own arrow function. That is the trade-off: arrow fields keep `this` bound but cost one function per instance.
questions.asked: It checks you know where class members actually live, which matters for memory and for `bind`-free handlers.

questions.code:
class User {}
const u = User();
questions.why: Class constructors cannot be called without `new`; doing so throws 'Class constructor User cannot be invoked without new'. That check is one of the real differences between `class` and an old constructor function, which would silently run with the wrong `this`.
questions.asked: It checks that you know classes are more than syntax sugar in a few safety-relevant ways.

questions.q: A subclass constructor assigns a field before calling `super`. What does `new Admin('Ada')` do?
choices: It creates an Admin with both properties
It throws a ReferenceError before `this.role` is set
It throws a SyntaxError when the class is defined
questions.why: In a derived class, `this` does not exist until `super()` has run, because the parent constructor creates the object. Touching `this` first throws 'Must call super constructor in derived class before accessing this'. It is a runtime error, not a parse error.
questions.asked: It checks you understand who allocates the object in a class hierarchy.

choices: It recurses until the stack overflows
questions.why: `super.describe()` calls the parent class's version of the method with the same `this`, so the override can extend the behaviour rather than replace it.
questions.asked: A basic check that you can extend a method instead of copy-pasting it.

questions.why: Static members live on the class (the constructor function) itself, not on instances or the prototype, so `o.count` is undefined. Instances reach statics through `Order.count` or `this.constructor.count`.
questions.asked: It checks you know where static members live, which matters when reading factory and registry code.

questions.why: `#value in x` is an ergonomic brand check (ES2022): it is true only for objects that were constructed by this class and therefore carry the private slot. A public `value` property does not count, and unlike `instanceof` it cannot be fooled by prototype tricks.
questions.asked: It is recent syntax; knowing it shows you understand private fields as per-object slots rather than hidden properties.

questions.q: What happens when the last line runs?
choices: It logs true, since both hold 5
questions.why: Private fields are class-scoped, so `equals` may read `#pence` on any Money, but reading a private field from an object that does not have that slot throws a TypeError rather than returning undefined. Guard with `#pence in other` first.
questions.asked: It checks you know private fields throw on foreign objects, which matters for equality and comparison methods.

questions.why: Assigning to `t.f` calls the setter, which stores 100 in the private field, and reading `t.f` calls the getter, giving 212. Accessors live on the prototype and private fields are not properties, so the instance has no own enumerable keys.
questions.asked: It checks you know accessors are prototype members, which is also why they vanish from `Object.keys` and spread.

questions.why: `finally` runs after the `return` expression is evaluated but before the function actually hands the value back, so the caller logs `saved` last. It is not skipped by `return`, which is why it is the right place to release a connection or lock.
questions.asked: Interviewers use it to check you trust `finally` for cleanup such as closing a DB connection even on early return.

questions.why: A `return` inside `finally` replaces whatever the `try` or `catch` was about to return (or throw). The `failed` value is discarded, which is why linters flag `no-unsafe-finally`: it can silently hide failures.
questions.asked: A strong answer names the lint rule and explains that a return in `finally` can swallow a thrown error entirely.

questions.q: Why do code reviewers ask for `throw new Error('Invalid email')` instead of `throw 'Invalid email'`?
choices: A thrown string is a SyntaxError in strict mode and ES modules
Strings are wrapped in an Error automatically, losing the text
A `catch` block only receives values that inherit from Error
An Error carries a stack trace, a name and a message for logs
questions.why: Any value can be thrown and caught, but only Error objects capture a `stack` and have a predictable `name`/`message`, so loggers and `instanceof` checks work. Throwing a string is legal everywhere; you just lose where it came from.
questions.asked: It checks whether you have debugged a production log that said only "Invalid email" with no idea which line threw it.

questions.why: `name` is inherited from `Error.prototype`, where it is the string `Error`; subclassing does not change it. The instance still inherits from Error, so `instanceof Error` is true. Set `this.name` in the constructor (or as a class field) to get `NotFoundError` in logs.
questions.asked: Interviewers want to hear that custom errors need an explicit `name`, or every log line and error tracker groups them as plain `Error`.

questions.q: A `ValidationError extends Error` class should report its own type in logs and keep a field list. Which constructor is correct?
questions.why: A derived constructor must call `super` before touching `this`, and `Error` takes the message (plus an options bag) as its arguments, not a name. `Error.call(this)` does nothing useful for a class instance and never initialises it.
questions.asked: A strong answer also mentions passing `{ cause }` through `super(msg, { cause })` so the original error is kept.

questions.why: Reading a property of `null` or `undefined` throws a TypeError; the variable exists, its value just has no properties. ReferenceError is for names that are not declared at all.
questions.asked: This is the most common production crash in JavaScript, and naming the error type correctly shows you have read real stack traces.

questions.q: A typo sneaks into a function. What does this log?
questions.code:
let total = 0;
try { totl += 1; } catch (e) { console.log(e.name); }
questions.why: `totl` is not declared anywhere, so reading it for `+=` throws a ReferenceError at runtime. It is not a SyntaxError because the code parses fine, and not a TypeError because there is no value to misuse.
questions.asked: Interviewers use it to see whether you can tell the error classes apart when triaging an alert.

questions.q: An Express handler wraps its body in `try { ... } catch (e) { console.log(e); res.json({ ok: true }); }`. What is the real problem?
choices: `console.log` cannot print Error objects, so the log line is empty
Express catches the error first, so the `catch` block never runs
The failure is swallowed: the client sees success and nothing alerts
The response is sent twice, so Express throws ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT
questions.why: Catching an error and replying as if it succeeded hides the failure from the caller and from monitoring. Either handle it meaningfully (e.g. a 4xx/5xx problem response) or rethrow/`next(err)`. `console.log` prints errors fine, and only one response is sent here.
questions.asked: A strong answer describes an error strategy: expected errors map to 4xx, unexpected ones propagate to a central handler that logs and returns 500.

questions.why: An exception thrown in `finally` replaces the one that was propagating, so the original `upload rejected` is lost. JavaScript never merges them into an AggregateError; if both matter, catch the cleanup error and attach the original as `cause`.
questions.asked: It separates people who have lost the real root cause to a failing cleanup step from those who have only read about `finally`.

questions.q: A payment SDK throws plain objects. What does this log?
questions.code:
try { throw { code: 'E_LIMIT' }; }
catch (e) { console.log(e.message, e.code); }
questions.why: Anything can be thrown, and `catch` receives it unchanged. A plain object has no `message` property, so it logs `undefined`. That is why a global handler should not assume `err.message` or `err.stack` exist.
questions.asked: A strong answer mentions normalising unknown thrown values (`err instanceof Error ? err : new Error(String(err))`) at boundaries.

choices: 2 email required, age must be positive
questions.why: `AggregateError` takes an iterable of errors and a message; the errors are exposed on `.errors` and the message is exactly the second argument. It does not concatenate the child messages.
questions.asked: Interviewers use it to see if you know a standard way to report several validation failures at once.

questions.why: `defineProperty` defaults `enumerable`, `writable` and `configurable` to false, so `id` exists (`user.id` is 7) but `Object.keys` and `JSON.stringify` skip non-enumerable properties. Plain assignment would set all three flags to true.
questions.asked: It checks you know descriptor defaults, which explains "why is this field missing from my API response?" bugs.

questions.why: A getter runs every time the property is read, so it sees the pushed item and returns 15. It is not a cached value computed when the object was created, and reading it does not return the function.
questions.asked: Interviewers like a candidate who can say when a derived value belongs in a getter rather than stored state that can go stale.

questions.q: In an ES module, what happens on the second line?
questions.why: Assigning to an accessor property that has no setter fails; ES modules are always strict, so the failure throws a TypeError instead of being silently ignored. In a sloppy script it would log `paid`.
questions.asked: A strong answer contrasts the silent failure in sloppy mode with the loud one in modules and classes.

questions.q: Which call lets you still change existing property values, but stops properties being added or deleted?
questions.why: `seal` blocks adding and deleting but leaves values writable. `freeze` also makes every value read-only, and `preventExtensions` only blocks adding, so deletion is still allowed.
questions.asked: Interviewers ask it to see whether you know the three levels rather than treating "freeze" as the only option.

questions.why: Spread reads each own enumerable property once and copies the resulting value, so the getter runs once and `copy.n` is a plain data property holding 1. The getter itself is not copied, so later reads do not increment `reads`.
questions.asked: It exposes whether you know spread copies values, not property definitions, which matters when copying class instances or models with accessors.

questions.why: Properties created by assignment or a literal get `writable`, `enumerable` and `configurable` all true. `defineProperty` defaults every flag you omit to false, so `b` is read-only.
questions.asked: Interviewers use it to check you understand that the two ways of creating a property are not equivalent.

questions.why: Every `Symbol()` call creates a new unique value; the description is only a label. `Symbol.for` looks the key up in a global registry and returns the same symbol each time.
questions.asked: A strong answer says when you would want a registered symbol (sharing across modules or realms) versus a private unique one.

questions.why: Symbol-keyed properties are skipped by `Object.keys`, `for...in` and `JSON.stringify`, so they are handy for attaching metadata that must not leak into API responses. `Object.getOwnPropertySymbols` or `Reflect.ownKeys` still see them, so they are hidden, not private.
questions.asked: Interviewers like the nuance that symbols hide keys from serialisation but are not a security boundary.

questions.why: Unary `+` passes the hint `number`, a template literal passes `string`, and binary `+` passes `default`. The method returns the pound string for anything other than `number`, so both string forms print `£2.5`. `toPrimitive` takes priority over `valueOf`/`toString`.
questions.asked: A strong answer knows binary `+` uses the `default` hint, which is why `Date` objects concatenate as strings.

choices: A TypeError on the first line
questions.why: `String(symbol)` is an explicit conversion and returns `Symbol(draft)`, but implicit conversion via `+` or a template literal throws `TypeError: Cannot convert a Symbol value to a string`. That asymmetry is deliberate, to stop symbols leaking into strings by accident.
questions.asked: Interviewers use it to test whether you know explicit and implicit coercion can behave differently for the same value.

questions.why: Spread and `for...of` stop when the iterator reports `done: true`, and the value that comes with it (the `return` value) is discarded. Only `yield`ed values are collected.
questions.asked: A strong answer knows the return value is only visible when you call `next()` yourself.

questions.q: An error is logged by a JSON logger. What does this log?
choices: RangeError: page must be at least 1, then {}
page must be at least 1, then {"message":"page must be at least 1"}
RangeError: page must be at least 1, then {"name":"RangeError"}
questions.why: `Error.prototype.toString` gives `name: message`, but `message` and `stack` are own non-enumerable properties and `name` lives on the prototype, so `JSON.stringify` finds nothing to serialise and prints `{}`. Structured loggers therefore copy `name`, `message`, `stack` and `cause` explicitly.
questions.asked: It explains the classic empty `"error": {}` in log aggregators and shows you know how errors are serialised.

questions.q: A helper returns a generator of unpaid order ids. What does this log?
questions.why: A generator object is a one-shot iterator: `next()` consumes the first id and spread only collects what is left. Arrays differ because every `for...of` asks them for a fresh iterator, so return an array if callers need to iterate twice.
questions.asked: It catches the bug where a helper returns an iterator and the caller consumes part of it before looping.

questions.q: A booking API computes nights stayed. What does this log?
questions.why: Subtracting Dates coerces both to their millisecond timestamps, so the difference is 604,800,000 ms, which is 7 days. Using UTC instants avoids the DST hour that can make local-time day maths come out as 6.958.
questions.asked: Interviewers want to hear that date arithmetic is millisecond arithmetic and that UTC keeps it honest.

questions.q: A client sends `dueDate: "soon"`. What does this log?
questions.why: An unparseable string gives a Date whose time value is NaN; it prints as `Invalid Date`, and `toISOString` throws a RangeError. The constructor itself never throws, so you must validate with `Number.isNaN(d.getTime())`.
questions.asked: A strong answer validates dates at the API boundary rather than discovering the RangeError during serialisation.

questions.q: What is the safest way to send a date-time from a Node API to a browser in JSON?
choices: `date.toString()`, which includes the server time zone name
`date.toLocaleString()`, so the text matches the user's locale
An ISO 8601 UTC string, as produced by `date.toISOString()`
The Date object itself, which JSON keeps as a Date type
questions.why: ISO 8601 in UTC (`2026-09-24T10:00:00.000Z`) is unambiguous and round-trips with `new Date(str)` everywhere. JSON has no Date type, locale strings are for display only, and `toString()` output is not reliably parseable.
questions.asked: Interviewers expect "store and transmit UTC, format for the user at the edge".

questions.why: The comparator subtracts Dates, which coerces them to timestamps, giving a numeric ascending sort. Without a comparator, `sort` would compare their long string forms instead.
questions.asked: It is a quick check that you know the idiomatic way to sort by date.

questions.why: Date setters normalise overflowing fields, so day 35 of January rolls over to 4 February. Remember the month argument to `Date.UTC` is zero-based, so `0` is January.
questions.asked: Interviewers like it because "add N days" is a real feature and the overflow behaviour is both useful and surprising.

questions.q: A reminder for "same time tomorrow" is computed as `new Date(t + 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000)` on a server running in Europe/London. What happens on the night the clocks go forward?
choices: It fires an hour early, because that day has 25 hours
It throws a RangeError for the skipped hour
Nothing, since Date adjusts millisecond maths for DST
It fires an hour late on the wall clock, as the day has 23 hours
questions.why: Adding 86,400,000 ms is exactly 24 real hours, but the spring-forward day is only 23 wall-clock hours long, so 10:00 becomes 11:00. For calendar maths use `setDate(getDate() + 1)` in the user's zone (or Temporal where available).
questions.asked: A strong answer distinguishes elapsed-time arithmetic from calendar arithmetic and names the time zone the calculation should happen in.

questions.q: A component accepts an optional `onSave` callback. What does this log?
choices: TypeError: hooks.onSave is not a function
questions.why: `?.()` checks the function reference itself: if it is `null` or `undefined` the call is skipped and the expression evaluates to `undefined`. It would still throw if `onSave` were a non-function value such as a string.
questions.asked: Interviewers use it to check you know optional chaining works on calls, which replaces `if (onSave) onSave()` noise.

questions.q: An API returned `{ data: null }`. What does this log?
questions.code:
const res = { data: null };
console.log(res.data?.user.name, res.body?.items[0]);
questions.why: Optional chaining short-circuits the rest of the chain: once `res.data` is nullish, `.user.name` is never evaluated, so you only need `?.` at the point that can be missing. `?.` always yields `undefined`, never `null`.
questions.asked: A strong answer explains short-circuiting and warns against sprinkling `?.` on every segment, which hides real bugs.

questions.why: Arrow functions have no `arguments` object of their own; the name resolves lexically to `outer`'s `arguments`, which holds one value. Use rest parameters (`...args`) when you need an arrow's own arguments.
questions.asked: It checks that you know arrows borrow `this`, `arguments` and `new.target` from the enclosing function, not just `this`.

questions.code:
function createUser(name, role = 'user', ...tags) {}
console.log(createUser.length);
questions.why: `length` counts parameters before the first one with a default value, and never counts a rest parameter. Libraries such as Express read `fn.length` (four arguments means an error handler), so a default can change behaviour.
questions.asked: A strong answer connects `fn.length` to real framework behaviour rather than treating it as trivia.

questions.why: The name of a named function expression is bound only inside the function body, so recursion works but `fact` is not visible outside. It also gives stack traces a useful name.
questions.asked: Interviewers ask it to check you understand that expression names are scoped to the function, unlike declarations.

questions.why: Default expressions are evaluated at call time, and only when the argument is `undefined`. The second call passes 9, so `nextId` is not called and the counter is still 1 before the third call.
questions.asked: It shows whether you know defaults are lazy and per call, unlike Python's once-at-definition defaults.

questions.q: A memoised price lookup takes an options object. What does this log?
questions.why: `String({ base: 5 })` is `[object Object]` for every object, so both calls share one cache key and the second returns the first result. Build keys from the relevant fields (or `JSON.stringify` with stable ordering), or use a `Map`/`WeakMap` keyed by identity.
questions.asked: A strong answer names cache-key design as the hard part of memoisation and suggests a deliberate key function.

questions.q: A developer writes `const penalty = -rate ** 2;`. What happens?
choices: It is a SyntaxError until you add parentheses
It is a TypeError at runtime for negative rates
questions.why: The language forbids a unary operator directly before the base of `**` because maths and other languages disagree on the meaning. You must write `(-rate) ** 2` or `-(rate ** 2)`, and the file fails to parse otherwise.
questions.asked: Interviewers like it because the answer ("it will not even parse") shows you know the grammar, not just the runtime.

questions.why: Postfix `--` returns the old value and then decrements, so `shown` gets 5 and `stock` becomes 4. Prefix `--stock` would decrement first and return 4.
questions.asked: It is a quick check that you can read increment operators correctly in reviews.

questions.q: A status arrives from a query string. What does this log?
questions.why: `switch` compares with strict equality (`===`), so the string `'1'` never matches the number `1` and control falls to `default`. Convert the input with `Number(status)` first, or use string cases.
questions.asked: It catches the common bug where query-string values are compared to numeric constants.

questions.why: Without `break`, execution falls through from the matching case into every case below it, so an editor gets `edit` and `read`. Intentional fall-through like this should carry a comment, because linters flag it as a likely bug.
questions.asked: A strong answer knows fall-through is occasionally deliberate and mentions the `no-fallthrough` lint rule.

questions.q: A nested search should stop at the first stock level above 5. What does this log?
questions.why: `break search` exits the labelled outer loop, so the first value above 5 wins. A plain `break` would only leave the inner loop, and the next row would overwrite `found` with 8.
questions.asked: Interviewers use it to see if you know labels exist, and whether you would rather extract a function and `return`.

questions.why: `&&` and `||` return one of their operands, not a boolean: `&&` returns the first falsy operand or the last one, `||` the first truthy one or the last. So you get the empty name, the fallback, and `null`.
questions.asked: It checks you know these operators return values, which is why they work for defaults and guarded access.

questions.why: `a &&= b` assigns only when `a` is truthy, so the email is normalised and the empty phone is left untouched (not replaced by `false`). The property stays present, so it still appears in the JSON.
questions.asked: Interviewers like candidates who can pick between `&&=`, `||=` and `??=` for a given clean-up rule.

questions.why: `&&` stops at the falsy `isAdmin` and never calls `audit`, while `||` must evaluate its right side because the left is falsy. The comma operator in `audit` evaluates `audits++` and then returns `true`.
questions.asked: It exposes whether you would notice a side effect hidden inside a condition that sometimes does not run.

questions.q: Why might a CommonJS migration script be wrapped in `(async () => { ... })();`?
choices: It makes the whole file run in strict mode automatically
Top-level `await` is only available in ES modules, not CommonJS
Node refuses to run scripts that use `await` outside a class
It stops variables leaking into other modules' scopes
questions.why: CommonJS files are wrapped in a normal function, so `await` at top level is a SyntaxError; an async IIFE gives you an async context. In an `.mjs` file or `"type": "module"` package you can just use top-level `await`. CommonJS scope is already per file.
questions.asked: A strong answer also adds a `.catch` so a failure sets a non-zero exit code instead of an unhandled rejection.

questions.code:
function tagUser(id, ...roles) { return [id, roles]; }
console.log(tagUser(7), tagUser(7, 'admin', 'editor'));
questions.why: A rest parameter always receives a real array, which is empty when no extra arguments are passed; it is never `undefined`. It collects every remaining argument, not just the next one.
questions.asked: It checks the basics of rest parameters, which replaced the old `arguments` object in modern code.

questions.why: The `numeric: true` collation option compares digit runs by value, giving the natural order users expect. A plain `localeCompare` or default sort would put `invoice-10` before `invoice-2`.
questions.asked: Interviewers like it because "sort file names like a human would" is a real ticket with a one-option answer.

questions.q: An `Authorization` header is parsed. What does this log?
questions.why: The second argument to `split` caps how many pieces are returned; the rest of the string is discarded, not glued onto the last piece. If you need "split once", take `indexOf` and slice, or destructure the first two parts and rejoin.
questions.asked: It catches the assumption, common among Python developers, that the limit keeps the remainder in the last item.

questions.code:
const sku = 'TSHIRT-RED-XL';
console.log(sku.at(-1), sku.split('-').at(-1), sku[-1]);
questions.why: `at` accepts negative indexes counting from the end, on strings and arrays alike. Bracket access treats `-1` as a property name, which does not exist, so it gives `undefined`.
questions.asked: It is a quick check you know the modern way to read the last element without `length - 1`.

questions.q: A Windows path is built with a template literal. What does this log?
questions.code: console.log(String.raw`C:\new\table`.length, `C:\new\table`.length);
questions.why: In a normal template literal `\n` and `\t` are escape sequences for newline and tab, so the string is 10 characters. `String.raw` keeps the backslashes literally, giving 12. Better still, use forward slashes or `path.join` for paths.
questions.asked: Interviewers use it to check you know escape processing and the tool that turns it off.

questions.code:
const tag = (strings, ...values) => [strings.length, values.length];
console.log(tag`Order ${7} shipped to ${'Leeds'}`);
questions.why: A tag function gets the literal pieces around each placeholder (`"Order "`, `" shipped to "` and a trailing `""`) plus the interpolated values separately, so there is always one more string than value. That separation is what lets SQL and HTML tags escape values safely.
questions.asked: A strong answer explains why getting values separately makes injection-safe query builders possible.

questions.q: A date is reformatted for a UK invoice. What does this log?
questions.why: In a replacement string, `$<name>` inserts a named capture group (and `$1` a numbered one). Named groups make the reordering readable and survive someone adding another group to the pattern.
questions.asked: It checks you can use replacement patterns instead of reaching for split-and-join.

questions.why: `.*` is greedy and grabs as much as possible, backtracking only to the last ``. Adding `?` makes it lazy, so it stops at the first ``. For real HTML use a parser, not a regex.
questions.asked: Interviewers ask it to check you can explain greedy versus lazy quantifiers with a concrete example.

questions.code:
const s = 'SKU-12, SKU-7';
console.log(s.match(/SKU-(\d+)/)[1], s.match(/SKU-(\d+)/g));
questions.why: Without `g`, `match` returns the first match with its capture groups. With `g` it returns every full match but drops the groups, which is why `matchAll` exists when you need both.
questions.asked: It checks you know why `match` with `g` "loses" the capture groups.

questions.q: A search box must match the literal text a user typed, such as `price (USD)`, case-insensitively. Which is correct in Node 24?
questions.why: `RegExp.escape` (ES2025, available in Node 24) escapes every character that has meaning in a pattern, so parentheses match literally. Passing the raw term treats `(USD)` as a group, and URI or JSON encoding produce text that no longer matches the input.
questions.asked: A strong answer mentions that unescaped input is also a ReDoS risk, not just a matching bug.

questions.code: console.log(/^.$/.test('👍'), /^.$/u.test('👍'));
questions.why: Without `u`, a regex works on UTF-16 code units, and the emoji is two of them, so `.` cannot match it alone. The `u` (or newer `v`) flag makes the pattern work on code points.
questions.asked: Interviewers use it to see if you know to add `u` whenever user-entered text can contain emoji or non-Latin scripts.

questions.q: A formula string is tokenised. What does this log?
questions.code: console.log('a1b2c'.split(/\d/), 'a1b2c'.split(/(\d)/));
questions.why: When the separator pattern contains a capture group, `split` includes the captured text in the output between the pieces. That is a cheap way to keep delimiters when tokenising.
questions.asked: It separates people who know `split` well from those who reach for a hand-written loop.

questions.q: What is the pragmatic way to validate an email address on a sign-up form?
choices: A full RFC 5322 regex, so every legal address is accepted
A simple shape check, then a confirmation email to prove it
A DNS MX lookup on every keystroke to prove the domain
Checking only for `@`, since the server never needs to
questions.why: Real deliverability can only be proven by sending a message; a loose `something@something.tld` check catches typos without rejecting valid addresses. Giant RFC regexes are unreadable and still accept undeliverable addresses, and client checks never replace server validation.
questions.asked: Interviewers want to hear that validation is layered: cheap shape check, server check, then confirmation.

questions.code:
const csv = 'id,name\n1,Ada\n2,Grace';
console.log(csv.match(/^\d+/g), csv.match(/^\d+/gm));
questions.why: Without `m`, `^` only matches at the very start of the string, which is `i`, so there is no match and `match` returns `null`. With `m`, `^` and `$` also match at every line break.
questions.asked: It checks you know the difference between the `m` and `s` flags, which are often confused.

questions.q: Invoice totals are held as BigInt pence. What does this log?
questions.why: BigInt division truncates towards zero, so `7n / 2n` is `3n`, never a fraction. BigInt and Number are different types, so `===` is false, while loose `==` compares their mathematical values and is true.
questions.asked: A strong answer mentions that BigInt suits exact integer counters and ids, but splitting amounts still needs explicit rounding rules.

questions.q: A dashboard formats a revenue figure. What does this log?
questions.code: console.log((1234567.891).toLocaleString('en-GB', { maximumFractionDigits: 1 }));
questions.why: `toLocaleString` delegates to `Intl.NumberFormat`: British English groups thousands with commas and uses a dot for decimals, and the option rounds to one fraction digit. The dot-grouped form is what a `de-DE` locale would print.
questions.asked: Interviewers want to hear that you format numbers with Intl at the edge instead of hand-rolling regexes.

questions.why: `Intl.PluralRules` returns the plural category for a locale; in English only exactly 1 is `one`, so zero and fractions are `other`. Other languages have more categories (`few`, `many`), which is why a hard-coded `n === 1` check does not scale to translation.
questions.asked: It shows whether you know Intl has pluralisation built in, which matters the moment an app is localised.

questions.code:
const rtf = new Intl.RelativeTimeFormat('en', { numeric: 'auto' });
console.log(rtf.format(-1, 'day'), '|', rtf.format(3, 'hour'));
questions.why: With `numeric: 'auto'`, the formatter uses words such as "yesterday" and "tomorrow" where the locale has them; otherwise it prints "1 day ago". Future values read "in 3 hours" in English.
questions.asked: Interviewers like candidates who know "posted 3 hours ago" needs no library in modern runtimes.

questions.code:
const list = new Intl.ListFormat('en-GB', { type: 'conjunction' });
console.log(list.format(['Ada', 'Grace', 'Linus']));
questions.why: `Intl.ListFormat` joins items with the locale's conjunction rules. British English omits the serial (Oxford) comma, while `en-US` would print "Ada, Grace, and Linus".
questions.asked: It checks that you reach for the platform rather than writing `join` plus special cases for the last item.

questions.q: Which line is a SyntaxError in strict mode (and ES modules) but allowed in a sloppy script?
questions.why: Duplicate parameter names are rejected at parse time in strict code. Duplicate object keys have been legal in both modes since ES2015, and deleting `Object.prototype` fails at runtime (a TypeError in strict mode, `false` in sloppy mode), not at parse time.
questions.asked: A strong answer distinguishes parse-time strict errors from runtime ones such as writing to read-only properties.

questions.why: Inside a static method `this` is the class only when called as `Slug.make(...)`. Destructuring detaches the method, and class bodies are strict, so `this` is `undefined` and `this.clean` throws a TypeError. Referring to `Slug.clean` directly avoids the problem.
questions.asked: It checks you know static methods follow the same `this` rules as instance methods.

questions.why: The assignment goes through the setter, which stores 12 in the private field. Accessors live on `Product.prototype` and private fields are not properties at all, so the instance has no own enumerable keys.
questions.asked: Interviewers use it to check you know why such an object serialises to `{}` and needs a `toJSON`.

questions.why: Class methods are defined on the prototype as non-enumerable, so `for...in` (which does walk the prototype chain) skips them, and `JSON.stringify` only sees own enumerable data. Methods added with `X.prototype.greet = ...` would be enumerable and would show up in `for...in`.
questions.asked: A strong answer contrasts class syntax with the old prototype-assignment style, where methods leak into `for...in`.

questions.why: Class fields of a subclass are initialised right after `super()` returns, so while the base constructor runs the field does not exist yet. Pass the value to `super` or read it lazily if the base class needs it.
questions.asked: It separates people who know the construction order of fields from those who treat fields as prototype properties.

questions.why: Returning `this` from `add` makes it chainable, and both calls push onto the same private array, so the getter reports 2. Each `new Cart()` gets its own `#items`, because field initialisers run per instance.
questions.asked: Interviewers like it as a quick check of fluent APIs and per-instance field initialisation.

questions.why: `extends` sets up two chains: instances inherit through `Dog.prototype` → `Animal.prototype`, and the constructor itself inherits from `Animal`, which is how static methods are inherited.
questions.asked: A strong answer explains that the second chain is why `Dog.create()` works when only `Animal` defines `static create()`.

questions.why: `JSON.parse` only ever produces plain objects and arrays; nothing links the result to your class. To get methods back you must construct it, e.g. `Object.assign(new User(), data)` or a static `fromJSON`.
questions.asked: It catches the misconception that typing a response as `User` in TypeScript makes it a `User` instance at runtime.

questions.q: A `Person → User → AdminUser → SuperAdminUser` hierarchy keeps gaining flags. What is the usual mid-level recommendation?
choices: Add an abstract base class above Person to hold the shared flags
Prefer composition: pass small role or permission objects in
Replace the classes with prototype chains built by Object.create
Merge every class into one with a `type` switch in each method
questions.why: Deep inheritance couples every level to its parents' internals; composing behaviour from small objects or functions (e.g. a permissions policy injected into a user service) keeps each piece testable. Using `Object.create` just rewrites the same hierarchy.
questions.asked: Interviewers want a concrete example of when inheritance is still fine (framework base classes, error types) alongside the composition argument.

questions.why: Methods on the prototype are stored once and shared by every instance, and `this` is set per call to the object before the dot. Defining the function inside the constructor would give each instance its own copy.
questions.asked: It checks you understand what `class` desugars to and why shared methods save memory.

questions.why: Assigning creates an own property that shadows the inherited one; `delete` removes only the own property, so lookup falls back to the prototype again. `delete` never walks up the chain.
questions.asked: Interviewers use it to test property lookup and shadowing, the core of the prototype model.

questions.why: Each call to `createIdGenerator` creates a fresh `n` and `prefix`, and the returned closure keeps its own copy alive. The two generators therefore count independently.
questions.asked: A strong answer names the pattern (factory plus closure) and when a class would be clearer.

questions.why: Function declarations are hoisted with their value, and a `var` of the same name does not reset it, so the first line sees a function. The assignment on line 2 then runs and overwrites it with a string.
questions.asked: It checks you can reason about hoisting precisely, and why `let`/`const` make such name clashes an early error.

questions.q: Which check reliably detects an array, including one created in an iframe or a Node `vm` context?
questions.why: Each realm has its own `Array` constructor, so `instanceof` and `constructor` checks fail for arrays from another realm; `typeof` is `object` for all arrays. `Array.isArray` checks the internal array type and works everywhere.
questions.asked: Interviewers ask it to see whether you know why `instanceof` is unreliable across realms.

questions.q: A quantity arrives as the string `'0'`. What does this log?
questions.why: Every non-empty string is truthy, so the first check passes. Loose equality converts both sides to numbers, and `0 == 0`, so the second passes too. Convert once with `Number(qty)` and compare numbers.
questions.asked: It is a compact demonstration of why truthiness and `==` disagree, and why you parse inputs at the boundary.

questions.code:
const start = new Date('2026-01-01T00:00:00Z');
console.log(typeof (start + 1), typeof (start - 1));
questions.why: Binary `+` converts a Date with the `default` hint, which Dates treat as `string`, so it concatenates. `-` only works on numbers, so the Date becomes its timestamp. Use `start.getTime() + ms` to be explicit.
questions.asked: A strong answer explains the `default` hint rather than just memorising the result.

questions.q: Empty form fields are converted with `Number`. What does this log?
questions.code: console.log(Number(null), Number(undefined), Number([]), Number(['7']));
questions.why: `null` converts to 0 and `undefined` to NaN. Arrays convert via their string form: `[]` becomes `''` (0) and `['7']` becomes `'7'` (7). So a missing value can silently become a real zero.
questions.asked: Interviewers use it to show why "missing" must be checked before numeric conversion in validators.

questions.q: A helper rounds to two decimal places. What does this log?
questions.code: console.log(Math.round(1.005 * 100) / 100, Math.round(1.015 * 100) / 100);
questions.why: `1.005` is stored as slightly less than 1.005, so `1.005 * 100` is `100.49999999999999` and rounds down; `1.015 * 100` is likewise just under 101.5. The fix for money is to hold integer minor units, or round with a decimal library.
questions.asked: A strong answer knows multiply-round-divide is not a fix, only a smaller version of the same float problem.

questions.q: A £100.00 bill (10,000 pence) is split three ways. What does this log?
questions.why: Each share gets the floored amount and the leftover pence (`10000 % 3 = 1`) are handed out one each to the first shares, so the parts always sum back to the total. Rounding each share independently would lose or invent a penny.
questions.asked: Interviewers ask about "splitting a bill" to see if you think about the pennies that do not divide evenly.

questions.q: A pasted price reads `1,299.00`. What does this log?
questions.code:
const raw = '1,299.00';
console.log(parseInt(raw), Number(raw), Number(raw.replaceAll(',', '')));
questions.why: `parseInt` stops at the first invalid character, so it returns 1; `Number` rejects the whole string and returns NaN. Stripping the grouping separator (for the expected locale) first gives 1299.
questions.asked: It shows whether you would notice a user's thousands separator turning £1,299 into £1.

questions.q: A refund leaves a tiny negative balance. What does this log?
questions.code:
const balance = -0.004;
console.log(balance.toFixed(2), Math.round(balance * 100) / 100);
questions.why: Rounding a small negative number keeps its sign: `toFixed` prints `-0.00` and `Math.round(-0.4)` is `-0`, which `console.log` shows as `-0`. Users then see "-£0.00"; normalise with `x || 0` or `x + 0` before display.
questions.asked: A strong answer knows negative zero exists and where it leaks into UI and CSV exports.

questions.q: A CLI prints a price list. What is the first line?
questions.why: `padEnd(8, '.')` fills to 8 characters on the right, giving `Tea.....`; `padStart(6)` left-pads `2.50` with spaces to 6 characters. Neither method ever truncates a longer string.
questions.asked: It checks you can build aligned text output without a library.

questions.why: Strings compare character by character. ISO `YYYY-MM-DD` puts the most significant part first, so text order matches date order; `DD/MM/YYYY` compares the day first, so `15/01` sorts after `01/02`. Store and compare ISO dates.
questions.asked: A strong answer mentions that this is why ISO dates in file names and database columns sort correctly.

questions.q: A search should treat accents and case as equal. What does this log?
questions.code:
const same = (a, b) => a.localeCompare(b, 'en', { sensitivity: 'base' }) === 0;
console.log(same('Resume', 'résumé'), same('Resume', 'Resumes'));
questions.why: `sensitivity: 'base'` makes the comparison ignore case and accents, so the first pair is equal. The extra `s` is a real difference at every sensitivity. `toLowerCase()` alone would still treat é and e as different.
questions.asked: Interviewers like it because accent-insensitive search is a real requirement with a one-line platform answer.

questions.q: What does `throw new Error('Order save failed', { cause: err })` give you over `throw new Error('Order save failed: ' + err.message)`?
choices: The original error object, with its own stack and type, stays attached
The new error inherits the class of `err`, so `instanceof` still matches
Node prints only the cause, hiding the less useful wrapper message
The wrapper reuses the stack of `err`, so the trace starts at the root
questions.why: `cause` keeps a reference to the original error, so loggers and `util.inspect` can print both stacks and code can still inspect `err.code`. Concatenating the message throws that away. The wrapper remains a plain Error with its own stack.
questions.asked: A strong answer explains wrapping at layer boundaries (repository → service) without losing the root cause.

questions.why: `floor` rounds towards minus infinity (-5), `trunc` just drops the fraction (-4), and `ceil` rounds towards plus infinity (-4). For positive numbers `floor` and `trunc` agree, which hides the difference until refunds or offsets go negative.
questions.asked: It checks you pick the right function when values can be negative, such as balance adjustments.

questions.q: A search term is put into a URL. What does this log?
questions.why: `encodeURI` is for whole URLs, so it leaves reserved characters such as `&` and `/` alone; `encodeURIComponent` escapes them, which is what a single query value needs. Neither uses `+` for spaces; that is form encoding, as produced by `URLSearchParams`.
questions.asked: A strong answer adds that `URLSearchParams` or `new URL()` avoid hand-encoding altogether.

questions.q: A value is pasted from a web page with non-breaking spaces. What does this log?
questions.code:
const pasted = '\u00a0 42 \u00a0';
console.log(pasted.trim().length, Number(pasted));
questions.why: `trim` removes all Unicode whitespace, including U+00A0, and `Number` applies the same whitespace rule before parsing, so both handle it. Hand-written `replace(/ /g, '')` would not, because it only matches the ordinary space.
questions.asked: It separates people who have debugged pasted spreadsheet data from those who assume a space is a space.

console.log(JSON.stringify([code.substring(6, 3), code.slice(6, 3)]));
questions.why: `substring` swaps its arguments when the start is greater than the end, while `slice` returns an empty string. `slice` also accepts negative indexes, which is why it is the one to prefer.
questions.asked: Interviewers ask it to see whether you know the quirks that make `slice` the safer default.

questions.q: A user has no middle name. What does this log?
choices: Ada null Lovelace, then Ada  Lovelace

Ada  Lovelace, then Ada null Lovelace
questions.why: Template literals convert `null` with `String()`, printing "null", whereas `join` turns `null` and `undefined` elements into empty strings (leaving a double space). The clean version is `[first, middle, last].filter(Boolean).join(' ')`.
questions.asked: It catches the "Hello null" bug that ships in emails and shows you know a tidy fix.

questions.code:
const text = 'Paid £25 and $30, owed £7';
console.log(text.match(/(?<=£)\d+/g));
questions.why: `(?<=£)` is a lookbehind: it requires a pound sign before the digits without including it in the match. The dollar amount fails the condition, and `g` returns every match.
questions.asked: A strong answer contrasts lookbehind with capturing the symbol and discarding it afterwards.

questions.q: A phone number is normalised. What does this log?
questions.why: `[^\d]` is a negated class matching any non-digit, and `g` replaces every occurrence with nothing, leaving only the digits. Without `g` only the first hyphen would be removed.
questions.asked: It is a quick check that you can read character classes and negation.

questions.q: A validator is called with missing values. What does this log?
questions.code:
const isSlug = (s) => /^[a-z-]+$/.test(s);
console.log(isSlug('summer-sale'), isSlug(null), isSlug(undefined));
questions.why: `RegExp.prototype.test` converts its argument to a string, so `null` becomes "null" and `undefined` becomes "undefined", and both are lowercase letters. Check the type (`typeof s === 'string'`) before testing.
questions.asked: Interviewers like it because it is a real validation hole that lets a missing field pass as a valid slug.

questions.q: A repository function looks up a user who may legitimately not exist. Which design is usually clearest for callers?
choices: Throw a NotFoundError for missing users and for database failures alike
Return an empty object `{}` so callers can read fields without checks
Return `false` for any failure so callers never need a `try` block
Return `null` when not found; throw only for failures like a lost connection
questions.why: "Not found" is an expected outcome, so returning `null` (or a result object) keeps it in normal control flow, while exceptions are reserved for things the caller cannot plan for. Returning `false` or `{}` hides real failures and invites `undefined` bugs further on.
questions.asked: A strong answer describes where the HTTP layer turns `null` into a 404 and exceptions into a 500.

questions.q: What does this log before it stops?
questions.code:
for (const id of [1, 2]) console.log(id);
for (const i = 0; i < 2; i++) console.log(i);
questions.why: `for...of` creates a fresh `const` binding per iteration, so it is fine. A classic `for` loop must update its variable with `i++`, which is an assignment to a constant: the body runs once with 0, then the update throws a TypeError.
questions.asked: It checks you understand why `const` works in `for...of` but not in a counting loop.
